dishes.name: Baked Apple
dishes.serviceNote: Breakfast tasting ($80) includes tasting portions and all listed drinks. Tree nuts (pecans), dairy; oats may carry gluten, confirm.

kept.q: How is the baked apple made?
kept.a: A whole apple, peeled and cored, baked until soft under a crumble of rolled oats, pecans, raisins, brown sugar and cinnamon, then glazed with brown sugar and served with sweetened creme fraiche. Warm, soft and cinnamon sweet, a gentle start to the breakfast. The cellar dossier calls its Auslese pairing the best block in the book.

value.s10: Our first course: a warm baked apple with oatmeal-pecan-raisin crumble, brown sugar glaze and sweetened crème fraîche.
value.s20: The Traditional Breakfast begins with a baked apple, filled with an oatmeal, pecan and raisin crumble, glazed with brown sugar and served with sweetened crème fraîche, like a warm apple crisp.
value.s45: Breakfast at Brennan’s has always been a long, celebratory meal, and the baked apple is a gentle start. The apple is baked until soft, with a crumble of oatmeal, pecans and raisins, then glazed with brown sugar. Sweetened crème fraîche, a slightly tangy cultured cream, balances the sweetness. It’s warm and comforting, and it comes after your Brandy Milk Punch eye opener, before the soup.

value.why: A brown-sugar glaze calls for a wine at least as sweet: the Auslese’s apple, apricot and honey mirror the fruit, and its acidity keeps a warm, sweet course fresh.
value.sayIt: The tasting includes its own drinks, but if you’d like wine, a half-bottle of Mosel Auslese tastes of baked apple and honey, and it carries you right through to the Bananas Foster.
value.whyThisWine: It’s a warm, sweet baked apple, so a sweet Riesling is the match. It’s honeyed but bright, like biting into a crisp apple, and it keeps the course light.
value.palate: Brown-sugar glaze makes a dry wine taste tart; the Auslese is sweeter than the glaze, so the apple tastes richer and the wine stays lush. Its acidity mirrors the apple’s own tartness and cuts the crème fraîche, while honey and apricot bridge to the raisins and caramel. Low alcohol keeps it gentle for the first course of breakfast.
value.secondWhy: A lighter glass of the Berres Riesling, taste it first: if it’s off-dry it works; if it’s dry, the glaze will make it taste tart.
value.serve: The Traditional Breakfast includes a Brandy Milk Punch here; offer wine only as an extra. The 375 ml half-bottle carries through to Bananas Foster, 2 to 3 oz pours in a small glass.
value.avoid: Avoid dry sparkling and dry reds: the brown sugar makes them taste sour and thin.
value.zeroProofWhy: For guests skipping the milk punch, its cardamom-clove syrup echoes the baked-apple spice.

value.s20: Our fourth course is a petite filet mignon with a potato rösti, a crisp, Swiss-style shredded potato cake, and garlic spinach, poured with Domaine de Châteaumar’s Côtes du Rhône.
value.s45: The last savory course is the steak, a classic part of a grand New Orleans breakfast. It’s a petite filet mignon, the most tender cut, with a potato rösti, a Swiss-style cake of shredded potato fried golden and crisp, and garlicky wilted spinach. We pour a four-ounce glass of Domaine de Châteaumar’s ‘Cuvée Vincent’ Côtes du Rhône, juicy, soft and just right for red meat at breakfast.

value.why: A soft, juicy old-vine Syrah from the Southern Rhône has fruit for the filet without heavy tannin at breakfast.
value.sayIt: This course comes with a glass of Côtes du Rhône, juicy and soft, perfect for the filet.
value.whyThisWine: This course comes with a Côtes du Rhône. It’s juicy and soft, enough for the steak but not heavy for breakfast, and the pepper in the wine picks up the garlic spinach.
value.palate: Lean filet can’t soften big tannin, but this Syrah’s soft tannins meet its protein gently, and the beef tastes juicier. Black raspberry fruit lifts the mild meat, and the wine’s pepper picks up the garlic in the spinach. The rösti’s fried richness is cleaned up by the wine’s fresh acidity, so the course stays savory and light enough for the morning.
value.secondWhy: A more structured Bordeaux if a guest wants to upgrade to a fuller glass.
value.stepUp: Inglenook Rubicon 2010 by the glass: aged Cabernet blend, now silky, with cedar and tobacco, a luxurious filet upgrade.
value.serve: Included 4 oz pour on the Traditional Breakfast; pour as the course fires. Slightly cool, 58 to 60°F, standard red glass. Take filet temperatures with the tasting order.
value.avoid: Avoid young, powerful Napa Cabernet: the lean filet can’t tame its tannin, and it overwhelms a breakfast portion.
value.zeroProofWhy: agave, basil and lime brighten the garlic spinach and rösti.

dishes.name: Louisiana BBQ Lobster
dishes.serviceNote: Shellfish (lobster), pork (’nduja), dairy (butter). Moderate heat. Confirm the kitchen’s BBQ sauce at lineup. Dinner tasting: $80, wine pairing $120 (4 oz pours).

kept.q: Which white is poured with the lobster tonight?
kept.a: With the lobster we pour a white Burgundy, Chardonnay with body for the lobster and butter and a fresh finish against the spicy nduja. Check the supplement card for tonight's producer before naming it: the website lists Domaine Matrot Meursault 2023, the September card listed Fichet Macon-Ige 2024. By the heat rule the Berres Riesling is the sharper tool for the nduja: if it runs hot, the Berres is lighter and a touch sweeter, and we can swap it.

say.value: Say it as it reads: Louisiana BBQ Lobster.

guest.value: Our Louisiana BBQ Lobster is lobster done in the New Orleans barbecue style, over a white bean stew with ’nduja, a soft, spicy Calabrian pork sausage that melts into the beans.

why.value: Sweet, buttery lobster with a spicy, smoky, creamy base.

pairs.value: First pick: Fichet ‘Château London’ Mâcon-Igé 2024, a tasting pour. Without alcohol: Black Hills.

value.technique: New Orleans barbecue-style

value.s10: Our second course: Louisiana BBQ lobster with a white bean stew and ’nduja, a spicy Calabrian sausage.
value.s20: Our Louisiana BBQ Lobster is lobster done in the New Orleans barbecue style, over a white bean stew with ’nduja, a soft, spicy Calabrian pork sausage that melts into the beans.
value.s45: New Orleans “barbecue” isn’t a smoker or a tomato sauce, it’s the buttery, peppery style made famous by barbecue shrimp. Here it’s lobster, which is sweet and rich. It sits on a white bean stew with ’nduja, en-DOO-yah, a spreadable, spicy pork sausage from Calabria in southern Italy, which melts into the beans and gives them a warm, red-pepper heat. Rich, spicy and comforting. We pour a Mâcon Chardonnay from Burgundy with it.

value.why: A Mâcon Chardonnay has the body for lobster and butter, with freshness to reset the palate after the ’nduja.
value.sayIt: With the lobster we pour the Fichet Mâcon-Igé, Chardonnay with body for the lobster and a clean finish against the spice.
value.whyThisWine: Lobster and Chardonnay are a classic, and this Mâcon is round enough for the butter but fresh enough for the spicy ’nduja. It makes the lobster taste even sweeter.
value.palate: Lobster’s sweetness and butter want a round white, and the Mâcon matches that texture. The ’nduja is the risk: the wine’s fresh acidity cuts the pork fat, and its moderate alcohol keeps the chile from flaring. The beans’ creaminess echoes the wine’s roundness, while the apple-citrus fruit makes the lobster taste sweeter. The finish is clean, ready for the redfish.
value.secondWhy: Off-dry-leaning Riesling for a guest sensitive to the ’nduja’s heat.
value.stepUp: Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin: the same region with finer, chalkier precision from one of Burgundy’s great estates.
value.serve: Included 4 oz pour on the $120 dinner-tasting pairing, pour just before the course lands. 50 to 53°F in a white-wine glass.
value.avoid: Avoid heavily oaked, high-alcohol Chardonnay: oak and alcohol amplify the ’nduja’s heat, and the pairing turns hot and heavy.
value.zeroProofWhy: lime and basil cool the ’nduja and cut the butter.

dishes.name: Roasted Rohan Duck Breast
dishes.serviceNote: Duck is usually served medium-rare to medium, confirm the kitchen’s standard and mention it. Tree nuts (hazelnuts). Dinner tasting course four.

kept.q: Which duck plate is on the dinner tasting tonight?
kept.a: Course four is Rohan duck, a specialty duck raised for rich, rosy meat. Confirm tonight's preparation with the kitchen before describing it: the website now lists a hazelnut crust with sweet potato puree, winter squash and sage, while the late summer menu had cane syrup glazed peaches and candied hazelnuts. Do not say peaches or squash from memory.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: A young Napa Cabernet against cane syrup peaches is a real tension and the guide admits it. From the list the Durban is the better technical red: ripe fruit, round tannin, body for the fat. The guide's avoid line excludes tart light reds while its second choice is a light Bourgogne; a ripe 2023 Bourgogne is not tart, which is why it stands.

dishes.description: Cane syrup-glazed peaches, candied hazelnuts

guest.value: Our fourth course is roasted Rohan duck breast with peaches glazed in Louisiana cane syrup and candied hazelnuts, rich duck, sweet fruit and a little crunch.

why.value: Rich, rosy duck with sweet, caramel-glazed fruit and crunch.

pairs.value: First pick: Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet Sauvignon 2021, a tasting pour. Without alcohol: Catalina Island.

value.technique: roasted
value.sides: candied hazelnuts
value.taste: rich, rosy duck with sweet, caramel-glazed fruit and crunch

value.s10: Roasted Rohan duck breast with cane syrup-glazed peaches and candied hazelnuts.
value.s20: Our fourth course is roasted Rohan duck breast with peaches glazed in Louisiana cane syrup and candied hazelnuts, rich duck, sweet fruit and a little crunch.
value.s45: Duck and fruit is a French classic, and this is the Louisiana version. Rohan is a special cross raised in New York for its tender, rosy meat, and the breast is roasted so the skin renders and the meat stays rosy. The peaches are glazed with cane syrup, Louisiana’s own sugarcane syrup, lighter and more buttery than molasses, so they’re sweet with a deep caramel note. Candied hazelnuts add crunch. We pour Paul Hobbs Cabernet from Coombsville in Napa with it.

value.why: Cabernet’s dark fruit and structure stand up to rich duck, and its ripeness meets the cane-syrup peaches.
value.sayIt: With the duck, the Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet, dark fruit for the peaches and structure for the rich meat.
value.whyThisWine: Duck breast is rich enough for Cabernet, and this one from Coombsville has dark fruit for the glazed peaches and structure for the duck. It stays fresh, so it doesn’t feel heavy.
value.palate: Duck breast is red and fatty enough to carry Cabernet: the tannin binds with fat and protein, and the wine tastes rounder. Ripe dark fruit keeps pace with the cane-syrup peaches, and Coombsville freshness stops it turning jammy. The glaze’s sweetness can firm up tannin, so let the fruit lead, duck and peach in the same bite. The candied hazelnuts echo the cocoa.
value.secondWhy: Pinot Noir and duck is the classic lighter match.
value.serve: Included 4 oz pour on the dinner-tasting pairing; open the bottle 30 to 60 minutes ahead. 60 to 64°F in a Bordeaux glass. For a guest who wants Pinot, offer the Bourgogne.
value.avoid: Avoid lean, high-acid whites and tart light reds: the cane-syrup glaze makes them taste sour and thin.
value.zeroProofWhy: watermelon and tonic refresh the palate after rich duck.

dishes.serviceNote: Coconut; eggs and dairy (curds); gluten and likely almonds (financiers are traditionally made with almond flour, confirm). Chia has a seedy texture, mention it for guests who dislike that. Sweet: suggest it to share.

say.value: Say it as it reads: Blackberry Trifle.

guest.value: Our Blackberry Trifle layers blackberry curd and lemon curd with coconut chia pudding and little blackberry financier biscuits: bright, tart and creamy, a lovely lighter way to begin breakfast.

why.value: Bright, tart, creamy and lightly sweet.

pairs.value: First pick: Dr. Hermann ‘Erdener Prälat’ Riesling Auslese 2014 (375 ml), $80 half-bottle. Without alcohol: Catalina Island.

value.technique: layered as a trifle
value.sides: blackberry financier biscuits, small, buttery almond cakes
value.taste: bright, tart, creamy and lightly sweet

value.s10: A sweet start: blackberry trifle with coconut chia pudding, lemon curd and blackberry financiers.
value.s20: Our Blackberry Trifle layers blackberry curd and lemon curd with coconut chia pudding and little blackberry financier biscuits: bright, tart and creamy, a lovely lighter way to begin breakfast.
value.s45: It’s one of our sweet starters, and a nice one to share. A trifle is a layered dessert, and ours goes blackberry curd, lemon curd and coconut chia pudding, chia seeds soaked until they turn into a soft, spoonable pudding, with blackberry financiers, which are small, buttery almond cakes, for texture. It’s tart and fruity more than sugary, so it wakes you up rather than weighing you down. Put it in the middle of the table while you look at the egg dishes.

value.why: The curds are sweet and tart, so the wine must be sweeter and just as acidic: the Mosel Auslese’s honeyed fruit and electric acidity match the lemon and blackberry without turning sour.
value.sayIt: If you’d like wine with it, a half-bottle of Mosel Auslese is lovely: honeyed and sweet, with bright acidity for the curds, and it carries on to dessert.
value.whyThisWine: The trifle is sweet and tangy, so I’d pour a sweet Riesling from Germany’s Mosel. It’s honeyed but racy, so the lemon and blackberry taste brighter instead of making the wine taste sour.
value.palate: A dry wine beside the curds tastes sour and thin; the Auslese is sweeter than the dish, so the curds taste fruitier and the wine stays lush. Its acidity matches the lemon’s tang point for point, and the honeyed stone fruit links blackberry to coconut. Because the alcohol is low, nothing burns against the cool cream, and the acidity lifts the chia pudding so the finish stays bright.
value.secondWhy: No dry wine on the list beats the Auslese with the berry curds. For a guest set on dry bubbles, say plainly that the sweet curds will make it taste drier and tarter and let them choose; otherwise offer the Catalina Island.
value.serve: Sold as a 375 ml half-bottle, about four dessert pours. Suggest it when the table orders sweet starters, it carries on to Bananas Foster. Small white or dessert glass, 2 to 3 oz.
value.avoid: Avoid Brut sparkling and crisp dry whites: next to sweet curds they taste sour, thin and hard.
value.zeroProofWhy: watermelon and tonic keep a sweet starter light and refreshing.

value.s10: Framboise French Toast, our citrus brioche with mascarpone mousse, raspberry coulis and local raspberries.
value.s20: Framboise is French for raspberry. We make French toast from our housemade citrus brioche and finish it with mascarpone mousse, a raspberry coulis and fresh local raspberries, soft, rich and bright.
value.s45: Framboise, frahm-BWAHZ, is French for raspberry, and that’s the star here. We bake our own citrus brioche, a rich, buttery egg bread, and turn it into French toast. Mascarpone, a rich Italian cream cheese whipped into a light mousse, adds richness, the raspberry coulis, a smooth fruit sauce, adds tartness, and fresh local raspberries go on top. It sits with our starters, so it’s perfect to share for the table, or as your sweet course.

value.why: Mascarpone mousse and raspberry coulis make this a sweet dish, so the wine must be sweeter: the Auslese’s honeyed fruit keeps the raspberries juicy and its racy acidity cuts the custardy brioche.
value.sayIt: With something this sweet a dry wine turns tart, a glass from a half-bottle of Mosel Auslese keeps the raspberries juicy and the brioche light.
value.whyThisWine: This is sweet, so a dry wine would taste sour next to it. The Mosel Riesling is honeyed but zippy, the raspberries stay juicy, and it keeps the rich brioche feeling light.
value.palate: The custard and mascarpone coat the palate; the Auslese’s acidity slices through and resets it. Because the wine is sweeter than the coulis, the raspberries taste bright and ripe rather than sour, and the citrus in the brioche links to the Riesling’s own citrus lift. Low alcohol keeps the combination light enough for morning, and the honeyed finish lingers over the berries instead of fading.
value.secondWhy: No dry wine on the list beats the Auslese with the mascarpone and coulis. For a guest set on dry bubbles, say plainly that it will taste drier next to the mousse and let them choose; otherwise offer the coffee with chicory.
value.serve: 375 ml half-bottle, about four dessert pours, ideal when a table shares sweet starters and wants to carry it to Bananas Foster. Pour 2 to 3 oz in a small white glass as the plate lands.
value.avoid: Avoid Brut sparkling and dry rosé, however festive: the coulis and mousse strip their fruit and leave them tart and hard.
value.zeroProofWhy: roast and gentle bitterness balance the sweet mousse and berries.

value.s10: Our Café Brûlot Coffee Cake: chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate, pecans, spiced citrus glaze and whipped crème fraîche.
value.s20: It’s named for café brûlot, New Orleans’ famous spiced coffee: a chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate cake with pecans, a spiced citrus glaze and whipped crème fraîche.
value.s45: Café brûlot is a classic New Orleans after-dinner coffee: flamed with brandy, orange and lemon peel, cinnamon and clove. This cake borrows those flavors: chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate in the cake, a glaze with citrus and warm spice, and pecans for crunch. Whipped crème fraîche, a slightly tangy cream, keeps it from being too sweet. It’s a great one to share with a cup of our coffee and chicory.

value.why: Banyuls’ cocoa, coffee and dried-fruit notes meet the chocolate and chicory, and it’s sweet enough that the cake won’t make it taste bitter.
value.sayIt: If you’d like a glass with it, Banyuls, a sweet red from the south of France, is a classic with chocolate and coffee. Otherwise, our chicory coffee is perfect.
value.whyThisWine: Chocolate and coffee make most wines taste bitter. Banyuls is a sweet red from the south of France with its own cocoa and coffee flavors, so the cake tastes even richer.
value.palate: Chocolate and chicory are bitter and drying; the Banyuls’ sweetness coats that bitterness so the cake tastes richer, not harsher. Its cocoa and coffee notes line up with the cake, and the black-cherry fruit plays like a Black Forest note against the spiced citrus glaze. The crème fraîche’s tang freshens each sip, and the fortified weight matches a dense cake instead of disappearing behind it.
value.serve: Banyuls is the dinner tasting’s dessert pour, confirm it can be poured at breakfast before offering. 2 to 3 oz in a small dessert glass, slightly cool; offer coffee alongside.
value.avoid: Avoid dry reds and Brut Champagne: chocolate and coffee turn tannin bitter and acidity sour.
value.zeroProofWhy: the classic, or the Café Glacé de la Maison if the guest wants it cold.

value.s20: Our Louisiana Oysters come in New Orleans BBQ sauce, which here means buttery and peppery, not smoky or tomato, with pickled collard greens, shallots and a crunchy fried saltine crumble.
value.s45: In New Orleans, “barbecue” doesn’t mean a smoker or a tomato sauce, it’s the style made famous by barbecue shrimp: a rich, buttery sauce with lots of black pepper and savory Worcestershire. We pair it with Louisiana oysters, then add pickled collard greens for a sharp, bright bite, shallots, and a fried saltine crumble for crunch. It’s rich and peppery, a real New Orleans flavor, and great to share before your eggs.

value.why: The buttery, peppery sauce wants a fuller white; a cool-climate Chardonnay brings the texture, and its acidity handles the pickled greens.
value.sayIt: With the oysters I’d pour the Gainey Chardonnay, creamy enough for the butter sauce, fresh enough for the pickled greens.
value.whyThisWine: The sauce is butter and black pepper, so I want a white with some body. This California Chardonnay is creamy but fresh, it matches the butter and keeps the pickled greens bright.
value.palate: The butter sauce and the Chardonnay’s creamy texture meet at the same weight, so neither thins out the other. Then the wine’s acidity picks up where the pickled collards leave off, cutting fat and resetting the palate. Pepper stays lively but doesn’t flare, because there’s no tannin to sharpen it. The oyster’s brine makes the fruit taste brighter, and the salty saltine crumble makes it seem riper.
value.secondWhy: Dry Champagne if they’d rather have bubbles cutting the butter.
value.stepUp: Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin: the same Chardonnay texture with more chalky finesse and precision against the pickle.
value.serve: Pour as the oysters fire. Serve around 50°F, less cold than a crisp white, so the creamy texture shows. Larger white-wine glass.
value.avoid: Avoid lean, green whites that the butter flattens, and tannic reds, tannin with oysters tastes metallic.
value.zeroProofWhy: lime and basil cut the butter sauce the way acidity would.

dishes.name: Creole Tomato Tostada
dishes.serviceNote: No meat listed, confirm with the kitchen for vegetarians. Dairy (burrata). Ask about gluten in the okra tostada. Seasonal: Creole tomatoes are a summer crop, so expect it to change as the season turns.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Confirmed: acid matches acid. Fresh tomatoes are tart, so the wine has to be bright too, and the burrata softens the edge.

dishes.description: Louisiana heirloom & Creole tomatoes, creamy burrata, housemade okra tostada, smoked tomato water

say.value: Say it as it reads: Creole Tomato Tostada.

guest.value: Our Creole Tomato Tostada celebrates Louisiana tomato season: heirloom and Creole tomatoes with creamy burrata on a crisp housemade okra tostada, with a smoked tomato water poured around.

why.value: Juicy, sweet-tart and creamy, with crunch and a hint of smoke.

pairs.value: First pick: Minuty ‘Prestige’ Côtes de Provence Rosé 2024, $17 the glass. Without alcohol: Catalina Island.

value.technique: served raw over a crisp housemade okra tostada
value.sides: creamy burrata
value.taste: juicy, sweet-tart and creamy, with crunch and a hint of smoke

value.s10: Louisiana Creole and heirloom tomatoes with creamy burrata on a housemade okra tostada, with smoked tomato water.
value.s20: Our Creole Tomato Tostada celebrates Louisiana tomato season: heirloom and Creole tomatoes with creamy burrata on a crisp housemade okra tostada, with a smoked tomato water poured around.
value.s45: Creole tomatoes are Louisiana’s summer tomato, juicy, sweet and a little tart, and here they’re mixed with heirlooms and served simply. Burrata is fresh mozzarella with a soft, creamy center, so it’s cool and rich against the acidity. The tostada, a crisp flat shell, is made in-house with okra, and smoked tomato water, a clear, intensely tomatoey broth, adds a whisper of smoke. It’s light, seasonal and gone when the tomatoes are, so I’d grab it now.

value.why: A dry Provence rosé has the acidity for raw tomato and the delicacy for burrata.
value.sayIt: With the tomatoes, the Minuty rosé from Provence is exactly right, dry, bright and refreshing.
value.whyThisWine: Fresh tomatoes are naturally tart, so the wine needs to be bright too. This Provence rosé is dry and delicate, it makes the tomatoes taste sweeter and loves the creamy burrata.
value.palate: Raw tomato’s acidity makes low-acid wines taste flat and oddly sweet. Provence rosé meets it with equal acidity, so the tomato tastes sweeter and juicier. The burrata’s cream softens the wine’s citrus edge, and the rosé’s red-fruit notes play off the smoked tomato water. The tostada’s crunch and the wine’s mineral finish leave the palate clean and cool, the way a summer tomato plate should.
value.secondWhy: Crisp Loire Sauvignon Blanc for its herbal, tomato-leaf freshness.
value.serve: Pour as the starter fires, well chilled, in a white-wine glass; keep the bottle iced. A great first glass on a warm evening.
value.avoid: Avoid oaky Chardonnay and tannic reds: tomato acidity makes oak taste bitter and tannin harsh, and both bury the burrata.
value.zeroProofWhy: watermelon and tomato are natural partners, and tonic’s lift matches the acidity.

dishes.name: Louisiana Crab Claws
dishes.serviceNote: Shellfish (crab), dairy (butter). Finger food, bring napkins and a plate for shells per house standard. Fines herbes is feen ZAIRB.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: With the crab claws the Leflaive Macon is the pour: its nutty richness mirrors the brown butter and its acidity meets the vinaigrette. For a guest who wants something leaner, the Durand Loire Sauvignon Blanc works because the dressing is a vinaigrette, so its acid has something to meet; that is not true of the BBQ butter on the oysters. For bubbles, the house Extra Brut or Rare. The Gainey Chardonnay is the lower priced creamy option, not a change of style; the dossier would lead with the Gainey and keep the Leflaive as the step up on both crab dishes once the Gainey is confirmed to read fresh rather than oaky.

kept.q: How do I describe the claws so nobody expects a cold cocktail claw?
kept.a: Our crab claws come warm, dressed in a brown butter vinaigrette, and you eat the meat straight off the claw. Say warm and off the claw when you describe them; use the pincer as a handle, bite and slide the cartilage out.

dishes.description: Warm brown butter vinaigrette, fines herbes

say.value: Say it as it reads: Louisiana Crab Claws.

guest.value: Our Louisiana Crab Claws come in a warm brown butter vinaigrette, nutty browned butter with a bright, tangy edge, finished with fines herbes, the classic French mix of delicate herbs.

why.value: Sweet crab with nutty butter, bright acid and soft herbs.

pairs.value: First pick: Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé 2022, $40 the glass. Without alcohol: Black Hills.

value.technique: served warm
value.sides: fines herbes: parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil
value.taste: sweet crab with nutty butter, bright acid and soft herbs

value.s10: Louisiana crab claws in a warm brown butter vinaigrette with fines herbes.
value.s20: Our Louisiana Crab Claws come in a warm brown butter vinaigrette, nutty browned butter with a bright, tangy edge, finished with fines herbes, the classic French mix of delicate herbs.
value.s45: Crab claws are a Louisiana favorite, sweet, delicate crab meat you pick up and eat right off the claw. We dress ours in a warm brown butter vinaigrette: butter cooked until it turns nutty and toasty, balanced with acidity so it’s rich but bright. Fines herbes, parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, finish it with a soft, fresh green note. It’s simple and elegant, and it’s great for the table to share.

value.why: White Burgundy’s nutty richness mirrors brown butter, and its acidity matches the vinaigrette and sweet crab.
value.sayIt: Brown butter and white Burgundy are a dream, the Leflaive Mâcon has that same nutty richness with a clean, bright finish.
value.whyThisWine: Brown butter and white Burgundy are a dream. The Leflaive has a gentle richness like the butter and bright acidity for the vinaigrette, it makes the crab taste sweeter.
value.palate: Brown butter’s nutty richness finds its echo in white Burgundy’s texture, so the two taste of each other. The vinaigrette’s acid would flatten a soft wine, but the Mâcon’s chalky acidity matches it, and the sweet crab tastes sweeter against the wine’s citrus. The fines herbes lift the wine’s floral notes. The finish runs butter, then lemon, then clean minerality.
value.secondWhy: A crisp Loire Sauvignon Blanc for a leaner match with the vinaigrette and herbs.
value.serve: Coravin pour, 50 to 54°F, in a white Burgundy bowl. Pour as the claws land, and bring the shell plate and napkins at the same time.
value.avoid: Avoid heavily oaked Chardonnay, oak plus brown butter turns heavy, and reds, whose tannin turns metallic with crab.
value.zeroProofWhy: basil and lime echo the fines herbes and cut the brown butter.

dishes.name: Grand Isle Jewel Oysters
dishes.serviceNote: Raw shellfish: give the consumer advisory: raw oysters carry risk, especially for guests who are pregnant, immunocompromised or have liver disease. Fresno chili is mild. Know the count per order. On the dinner tasting they’re paired with Charles Lafitte Brut.

kept.q: Catalina Island or Black Hills with the raw oysters?
kept.a: Keep the guide's Catalina Island as the printed pick: the mignonette already supplies acid and the tonic supplies the one thing the plate lacks, bubbles. A server may offer the Black Hills to a guest who wants lime and basil with the mignonette. Test both at lineup. Fresno is a red Californian chili from the 1950s, about the heat of a jalapeno but fruitier and thinner walled; preserved and stirred into the mignonette it gives a gentle warmth, not real heat.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Confirmed: salt and acid. The salt makes the wine taste fuller and the bubbles keep the oyster fresh. A chalky, Chardonnay-led vintage Champagne is a standard oyster step up, so the Rare stays.

dishes.description: Served raw, preserved Fresno chili mignonette, parsley

say.value: Say it as it reads: Grand Isle Jewel Oysters.

guest.value: Our Grand Isle Jewel oysters come from the Louisiana coast and are served raw, with a mignonette, the classic shallot-and-vinegar oyster sauce, made with preserved Fresno chili for a little warmth.

why.value: Clean, briny and cold, with a bright, gently spicy vinegar.

pairs.value: First pick: Brennan’s Essential by Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut NV, $28 the glass. Without alcohol: Catalina Island.

origin.value: Grand Isle Jewels are farmed oysters from Grand Isle on the Louisiana coast, raised in floating cages above the seabed and tumbled so they grow a deep cup and a clean shell. The brand brought the island's farmers together in 2025 and honors the late Jules Melancon, the first permitted to farm off bottom in 2012; the menu's singular Jewel is the plural brand Jewels. Clean, briny and cold, served raw with a preserved Fresno chili mignonette.

value.technique: served raw on the half shell
value.sides: parsley
value.taste: clean, briny and cold, with a bright, gently spicy vinegar

value.s10: Grand Isle Jewel oysters, served raw with a preserved Fresno chili mignonette and parsley.
value.s20: Our Grand Isle Jewel oysters come from the Louisiana coast and are served raw, with a mignonette, the classic shallot-and-vinegar oyster sauce, made with preserved Fresno chili for a little warmth.
value.s45: Grand Isle is a barrier island on Louisiana’s coast, and these oysters are named for it. We serve them raw, very simply, so you taste the oyster: clean, briny and cold. A mignonette is the classic raw bar sauce, vinegar, shallot and cracked pepper, and ours is made with preserved Fresno chili, so it’s tangy with just a gentle warmth. Parsley adds a green note. They open our dinner tasting, too, a perfect first bite with Champagne.

value.why: Bone-dry Extra Brut Champagne mirrors the brine, and its acidity matches the vinegar in the mignonette.
value.sayIt: Oysters and Champagne: our house Piper-Heidsieck is Extra Brut, so it’s very dry and crisp, perfect with the brine.
value.whyThisWine: Oysters and Champagne are a classic: the salt makes the wine taste fuller and the bubbles keep the oyster fresh. Ours is extra dry, so it’s crisp and clean, like a squeeze of lemon.
value.palate: Brine loves bubbles and acid. The oyster’s salinity makes the Champagne taste fuller and fruitier, while its acidity matches the mignonette’s vinegar so neither tastes sour. The mousse scrubs the palate after each oyster, and the chalky, bone-dry finish echoes the minerality of the shell. The chili’s warmth stays gentle, and the final impression is cold, clean and saline.
value.secondWhy: Albariño, with its salty, coastal snap, for a still white.
value.stepUp: If it is a special occasion, we pour Rare by the glass: Piper-Heidsieck's prestige vintage Champagne, Chardonnay-led from Grand Cru vineyards, kept fresh under a Coravin Sparkling stopper. It has the chalky precision raw oysters love, with toasted almond on the finish.
value.serve: On the dinner tasting, Charles Lafitte Brut is poured (4 oz). À la carte, pour Piper-Heidsieck as the oysters are shucked; tulip or white-wine glass, very cold.
value.avoid: Avoid oaked whites and all reds: oak turns bitter with brine, and tannin plus raw oyster tastes metallic.
value.zeroProofWhy: tonic’s bitter lift and bubbles do for brine what Champagne does.

dishes.name: Steak Tartare Cannoli
dishes.serviceNote: Raw beef and cured egg yolk, consumer advisory. Dairy (crème fraîche). Ask about gluten and the fryer for the potato shell. Handheld; suggest eating it in a couple of bites. Bottarga is boh-TAR-gah.

kept.q: What is the egg yolk bottarga, and is it on other dishes?
kept.a: The egg yolk on the Steak Tartare Cannoli is cured and grated over the top like bottarga, the Italian cured fish roe, for a rich, salty finish. It is the only dish on the current menus with it; do not mention the Ricotta Gnudi, which is off the menu.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Confirmed: bubbles and fat, and the rose rule is real, red fruit for raw beef.

dishes.description: Potato cannoli, crème fraîche, egg yolk bottarga

say.value: Say it as it reads: Steak Tartare Cannoli.

guest.value: Our Steak Tartare Cannoli is raw, finely chopped beef in a crisp potato shell shaped like a cannoli, with crème fraîche and a cured egg yolk grated over the top like bottarga.

why.value: Cool, silky beef in a crunchy shell, rich and savory.

pairs.value: First pick: Pierre Sparr Brut Rosé Crémant d’Alsace NV, $18 the glass. Without alcohol: Catalina Island.

value.main: Steak tartare, raw, finely chopped beef
value.technique: piped into a crisp potato cannoli shell
value.sides: grated cured egg yolk
value.taste: cool, silky beef in a crunchy shell, rich and savory

value.s10: Steak tartare piped into a crisp potato cannoli, with crème fraîche and grated cured egg yolk.
value.s20: Our Steak Tartare Cannoli is raw, finely chopped beef in a crisp potato shell shaped like a cannoli, with crème fraîche and a cured egg yolk grated over the top like bottarga.
value.s45: It’s a playful take on steak tartare. Tartare is raw beef, finely chopped and seasoned, and instead of toast we pipe it into a crisp potato shell shaped like a cannoli. Crème fraîche, a tangy cultured cream, keeps it cool and silky. The egg yolk is cured until firm and grated over the top, the way Italians grate bottarga, cured fish roe, it adds a rich, salty finish. Two or three bites, and a great way to start.

value.why: A Pinot Noir sparkling rosé has red fruit for raw beef and bubbles to cut the fried shell and crème fraîche.
value.sayIt: With the tartare I love a sparkling rosé, the Pierre Sparr is all Pinot Noir, so it has a little red fruit for the beef.
value.whyThisWine: It’s steak tartare in a crispy potato shell, so I love a dry sparkling rosé. It’s all Pinot Noir, a little red fruit for the beef and bubbles for the crunch.
value.palate: The potato shell brings fryer richness and the crème fraîche coats the palate; bubbles and acidity cleanse both. Raw beef has no char and little fat, so it wants red fruit rather than tannin, and Pinot Noir’s strawberry and currant meet it gently. The cured yolk’s salt makes the wine taste fruitier, and the finish is savory, bright and clean, ready for the next bite.
value.secondWhy: A light red Burgundy, low tannin, bright acid, for a still red.
value.serve: Pour as the starter fires; 43 to 46°F in a flute or tulip.
value.avoid: Avoid big, tannic reds: raw beef has no char or fat to soften tannin, so it turns astringent and metallic.
value.zeroProofWhy: tonic’s bubbles cut the fried shell and crème fraîche.

dishes.name: Turtle Soup
dishes.serviceNote: Contains alcohol (Sherry), flag it for guests avoiding alcohol. Egg; dairy (brown butter). Creole turtle soups are usually roux-thickened, so ask the kitchen about gluten. On the breakfast tasting, guests choose this or the gumbo (served with a Bloody Bull). Say “turtle” plainly, many guests are trying it for the first time.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Our house Champagne is Piper-Heidsieck's Extra Brut: very dry, with brioche and toasted nut from its time on the lees that pick up the Sherry while the bubbles clear the richness. For a step up, Rare is seventy percent Chardonnay with grilled almond and candied orange that meet the Sherry even more closely. Neither wine is oxidative; the Sherry echo is a fair secondary point behind dryness and bubbles.

dishes.description: 100% turtle meat, brown butter spinach, grated egg, aged Sherry

say.value: Say it as it reads: Turtle Soup.

guest.value: Our Turtle Soup is made with 100% turtle meat, with brown butter spinach and grated egg, and aged Sherry for a nutty lift at the end, rich, savory and very New Orleans.

why.value: A Brennan’s signature: deep, savory and meaty, with a nutty, bright finish.

pairs.value: First pick: Brennan’s Essential by Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut NV, $28 the glass. Without alcohol: Café Glacé de la Maison.

origin.value: It is made with farm raised Louisiana freshwater turtle, not wild or endangered turtle. Many New Orleans turtle soups, including the famous one at Commander's Palace, stretch the turtle with veal and beef; ours is 100 percent turtle meat, with brown butter spinach, grated egg and a splash of aged Sherry at the end.

value.technique: a rich, long-cooked Creole soup
value.sides: brown butter spinach and grated egg
value.taste: deep, savory and meaty, with a nutty, bright finish

value.s10: Our Turtle Soup: 100% turtle meat, brown butter spinach and grated egg, finished with aged Sherry. A Brennan’s classic.
value.s20: Our Turtle Soup is made with 100% turtle meat, with brown butter spinach and grated egg, and aged Sherry for a nutty lift at the end, rich, savory and very New Orleans.
value.s45: Turtle soup is one of the great Creole soups, and ours is made with 100% turtle meat. It’s deep and savory: if you’ve never had turtle, think of a rich, finely chopped stew. Brown butter spinach adds a toasty, earthy note, the grated egg adds richness, and aged Sherry brings a nutty, dry lift that cuts the richness. It’s also the soup on our Traditional Breakfast, so if you want one bowl that tells you what Brennan’s is about, this is it.

value.why: An Extra Brut Champagne’s bone-dry acidity and fine bubbles cut the soup’s richness, and its toasty depth echoes the aged Sherry.
value.sayIt: With the turtle soup I love a glass of our house Champagne from Piper-Heidsieck, it’s very dry, so it lifts the richness and picks up the Sherry.
value.whyThisWine: Turtle soup is rich and finished with Sherry. Our house Champagne is very dry, so the bubbles clean your palate between spoonfuls, and its toasty flavor picks up the Sherry, every bite tastes like the first.
value.palate: The first spoonful coats the palate with fat, gelatin and savory depth. The Champagne’s acidity and bubbles scrub that coating away, so the next spoonful tastes as vivid as the first. Its toasty, autolytic notes meet the nutty aged Sherry rather than fighting it, and because the wine carries almost no sugar it never turns sweet or cloying against the salty soup, the finish stays long, dry and clean.
value.secondWhy: For a still white: Leflaive’s Mâcon has the roundness to match the soup and the freshness to keep it lively.
value.stepUp: Rare by the glass, from the bottle under the Coravin Sparkling stopper: vintage depth, toasted almond and candied citrus that meet the aged Sherry even more closely.
value.serve: Pour as the soup is fired so the glass is waiting when the bowl lands. Tulip or white-wine glass; keep the bottle iced between pours.
value.avoid: Avoid tannic reds, salt and Sherry make tannin taste bitter and metallic, and oaky Chardonnay, whose vanilla sweetness muddies the nutty Sherry.
value.zeroProofWhy: chicory cold brew’s roast mirrors the Sherry’s nuttiness, or the Catalina Island for a bright, bubbly reset.

dishes.name: Seafood Gumbo
dishes.serviceNote: Shellfish (shrimp, crab, oysters) and pork (andouille). Gumbo is usually built on a roux, ask the kitchen about gluten. Mild to moderate spice. Breakfast tasting guests choose this or the turtle soup.

kept.q: Does the dining room gumbo follow the published recipe?
kept.a: Our published gumbo recipe starts with a dark mahogany roux, andouille and okra in crab stock, and the shrimp, crab and oysters go in at the very end so they stay tender; the published recipe carries okra, tomato and file, which the menu does not list, so say published recipe, never menu. Confirm at lineup that the dining room gumbo follows it before you say so to a guest.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: With the seafood gumbo I reach for the Berres Riesling: low alcohol, no tannin and a touch of sweetness, so it cools the andouille's spice and keeps the shrimp, crab and oysters tasting sweet. If the guest wants red, the Bourgogne Pinot Noir is light enough for the smoky sausage; it is the alternative, not the first choice.

dishes.description: Shrimp, crab, oysters, andouille, popcorn rice

guest.value: Our Seafood Gumbo is loaded with shrimp, crab and oysters, with andouille sausage for smoke and a little spice, over popcorn rice, a fragrant Louisiana long-grain that really does smell a little like popcorn.

why.value: A Brennan’s signature: savory, briny and smoky, with gentle spice.

pairs.value: First pick: C.H. Berres ‘Old Vines’ Riesling 2022, $14 the glass. Without alcohol: Black Hills.

value.technique: simmered into a Creole seafood gumbo
value.sides: Louisiana popcorn rice
value.taste: savory, briny and smoky, with gentle spice

value.s10: Our Seafood Gumbo: shrimp, crab and oysters with smoky andouille, over Louisiana popcorn rice.
value.s20: Our Seafood Gumbo is loaded with shrimp, crab and oysters, with andouille sausage for smoke and a little spice, over popcorn rice, a fragrant Louisiana long-grain that really does smell a little like popcorn.
value.s45: Gumbo is the dish that says Louisiana, and ours is all about the seafood: shrimp, crab and oysters, so you get sweetness and a little brine in every spoonful. Andouille, a coarse, smoked Cajun pork sausage, gives it a savory, smoky backbone and a gentle warmth. It’s served over popcorn rice, a Louisiana long-grain with a nutty, toasty aroma. It’s hearty, so it’s a great start before one of the egg dishes, and it’s the other choice on our Traditional Breakfast.

value.why: The Riesling’s high acidity and light body cut through the gumbo’s richness, and its ripe stone fruit cools the andouille’s spice.
value.sayIt: With gumbo I reach for Riesling, the C.H. Berres from the Mosel is light and bright, and it plays beautifully with the spice and the seafood.
value.whyThisWine: Gumbo has smoke and a little spice, so I like a light, bright Riesling. It’s refreshing, it calms the heat, and it lets the shrimp and crab taste sweet.
value.palate: The roux and andouille fat coat the palate while the spice builds slowly. Riesling’s high acidity cuts that richness, and its ripe stone fruit cushions the heat instead of amplifying it the way high alcohol would. With no tannin, the oysters and shrimp stay sweet rather than metallic, and the wine’s freshness makes the smoky sausage taste juicier. Each sip resets the heat, so the last spoonful isn’t hotter than the first.
value.secondWhy: A light red Burgundy works with the smoky andouille if they want red.
value.serve: Pour as the gumbo is fired. Taste this bottle at lineup so you can tell the guest honestly whether it’s dry or off-dry. Keep it well chilled, heat reads hotter with warm wine.
value.avoid: Avoid oaky, high-alcohol whites and tannic reds: alcohol magnifies the andouille’s heat, and tannin turns metallic with shellfish and bitter with spice.
value.zeroProofWhy: lime and basil cut the roux and cool the andouille’s spice.

dishes.name: Creole Caesar
dishes.serviceNote: Shellfish: the dressing is made with smoked oysters, always mention it; guests don’t expect shellfish in a Caesar. Dairy (Grana Padano), gluten (bread crisps). Ask the kitchen about raw egg and anchovy in the dressing.

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Confirmed: unoaked and saline, so the smoke does not turn bitter and the umami has no tannin to harden; the Extra Brut second is an equal.

dishes.description: Gem lettuce, smoked oyster dressing, Grana Padano cheese, Leidenheimer crisps

say.value: Say it as it reads: Creole Caesar.

guest.value: Our Creole Caesar is crisp gem lettuce tossed in a smoked oyster dressing, which gives it that deep, savory Caesar flavor, with Grana Padano and crisps made from Leidenheimer, New Orleans’ classic French bread.

why.value: Crisp, creamy, smoky and savory.

pairs.value: First pick: Pazo das Bruxas Albariño 2025, $16 the glass. Without alcohol: Catalina Island.

value.technique: tossed Caesar-style
value.sauce: smoked oyster dressing and Grana Padano
value.sides: Leidenheimer crisps, from New Orleans’ classic French-bread bakery
value.taste: crisp, creamy, smoky and savory

value.s10: Our Creole Caesar, crisp gem lettuce in a smoked oyster dressing, with Grana Padano and Leidenheimer crisps.
value.s20: Our Creole Caesar is crisp gem lettuce tossed in a smoked oyster dressing, which gives it that deep, savory Caesar flavor, with Grana Padano and crisps made from Leidenheimer, New Orleans’ classic French bread.
value.s45: It’s our Louisiana take on a Caesar. Gem lettuce is small, sweet and very crisp, so it holds up to a creamy dressing, and ours is made with smoked oysters, which bring a savory, smoky depth. Grana Padano, a nutty Italian hard cheese, adds salt and richness, and the crisps come from Leidenheimer, the bakery behind New Orleans’ po-boy bread. It’s a great, lighter start before an egg dish or the redfish.

value.why: Albariño’s citrus and saline snap match the smoked oyster dressing and cut through the cheese.
value.sayIt: With the Caesar I’d pour the Albariño, citrusy, with a salty edge that’s perfect with the smoked oyster dressing.
value.whyThisWine: The dressing is made with smoked oysters, so I want a seafood wine. Albariño comes from Spain’s Atlantic coast, lemony, with a little salty edge, and it keeps the creamy dressing light.
value.palate: The dressing’s tang would make a soft wine taste flat, but Albariño’s acidity meets it head-on and stays fresh. Salt from the Grana Padano and smoked oyster makes the wine seem rounder and fruitier, while its saline edge links to the oyster’s brine. The citrus cuts the creamy coating, and the smoke reads as savory rather than ashy. You finish on salt, lemon and sea, a clean slate for the next course.
value.secondWhy: Dry Champagne if the table is already drinking bubbles, salt and cream love bubbles.
value.serve: Pour as the salad is fired, well chilled, in a white-wine glass. Mention the smoked oyster dressing as you pour.
value.avoid: Avoid oaky, buttery Chardonnay and reds: oak turns bitter against smoke and acidity, and tannin goes metallic with the smoked oysters.
value.zeroProofWhy: tonic’s bitterness and bubbles cut the creamy dressing the way acidity would.

dishes.name: Eggs Hussarde
dishes.serviceNote: Eggs (soft poached yolks, and in the hollandaise), dairy, gluten, pork; the marchand de vin is made with red wine. Check with the kitchen before promising firmer eggs. Hussarde is hoo-SARD. On the breakfast tasting it comes with a 4 oz pour of Charles Lafitte Brut.

kept.q: Why is the second choice a still Pinot and not the pink bubbles?
kept.a: With Eggs Hussarde the house Champagne is the pour. For a guest who wants red, the Bourgogne Pinot Noir is light enough for the yolk and meets the red wine in the marchand de vin. For a guest who wants bubbles but something pink, the Pierre Sparr is all Pinot Noir, dry, with red fruit for the sauce.

value.s45: Eggs Hussarde is the New Orleans cousin of Eggs Benedict, and it’s the egg dish we’re known for. We make our own English muffins, and the Canadian bacon is cured with coffee, so it’s smoky and a little roasty. Then come two sauces: marchand de vin, “wine merchant’s sauce,” a savory red wine and mushroom sauce, and hollandaise, the buttery, lemony one. Rich, savory and bright all at once. It’s the heart of our Traditional Breakfast, so if it’s your first breakfast at Brennan’s, this is the one.

value.why: Dry Champagne’s acidity and bubbles slice through hollandaise and yolk, and its toasty notes suit the coffee-cured bacon.
value.sayIt: Eggs and Champagne are made for each other, our house Piper-Heidsieck is very dry, so it keeps the hollandaise feeling light.
value.whyThisWine: Eggs and hollandaise coat your palate, and Champagne clears it. Ours is very dry with fine bubbles, so the sauce stays rich but never heavy, and it’s lovely with the coffee-cured bacon.
value.palate: Yolk and hollandaise coat the tongue and blunt most wines. The Champagne’s acidity and bubbles lift that coating so each bite tastes fresh. The dry finish sharpens the salty, coffee-cured bacon, and the Pinot-based body stands up to the winey marchand de vin instead of disappearing. Toasty autolytic notes meet the toasted muffin, and the rhythm stays clean: rich bite, bright sip, repeat.
value.secondWhy: The marchand de vin is a red wine sauce, so a light Bourgogne Pinot Noir works for a guest who wants red.
value.stepUp: Rare by the glass, from the bottle under the Coravin Sparkling stopper: Chardonnay-led vintage Champagne with deeper toasted-almond richness, a celebration upgrade with the same clean cut.
value.serve: Pour as the eggs are fired. On the Traditional Breakfast the included pour is Charles Lafitte Brut, 4 oz, don’t double-pour. À la carte, Piper-Heidsieck by the glass in a tulip.
value.avoid: Avoid oaky Chardonnay, oak and hollandaise turn heavy and flabby, and firm-tannin reds, which taste metallic against egg yolk.
value.zeroProofWhy: tonic’s bubbles and bitterness cut hollandaise much as Champagne does.

The original was poached eggs on artichoke bottoms with hollandaise, anchovy, ham and truffle, with no spinach. The creamed spinach most kitchens use now came later. Ours fries the artichokes, makes the spinach with Parmesan and swaps hollandaise for Choron, a bearnaise with tomato.

value.s45: Eggs Sardou is one of the classic New Orleans egg dishes, it was created at Antoine's for the French playwright Victorien Sardou, and ours is the creamed spinach version. Ours pairs poached eggs with crispy artichokes and creamed spinach made with Parmesan. Instead of hollandaise, it’s finished with Choron sauce: a béarnaise, butter, egg yolk, shallot and tarragon, with tomato folded in, so it’s tangy and herbal. It’s rich, but the artichokes and tomato keep it bright. It’s also our meatless egg dish.

value.why: Artichokes make many wines taste sweet or metallic; a crisp, herbal Loire Sauvignon Blanc stands up to them and cuts the creamed spinach.
value.sayIt: Artichokes are tricky with wine, but a Loire Sauvignon Blanc loves them, the Durand is crisp and herbal.
value.whyThisWine: Artichokes are tricky, they make many wines taste strange. This Loire Sauvignon Blanc is crisp and herbal, so it loves the artichokes and the tarragon in the sauce, and it lightens the creamed spinach.
value.palate: Artichoke normally makes wine taste oddly sweet and flat. A bone-dry, high-acid Sauvignon Blanc has little fruit sweetness to exaggerate, so it survives, and its green, herbal flavors join the artichoke and tarragon instead of fighting them. The acidity cuts through the creamed spinach and Choron, and the vinegar in the sauce matches the wine’s own bite. The finish stays crisp and herbal, not muddy.
value.secondWhy: Sparkling rosé if the table is already celebrating.
value.serve: Pour as the eggs fire, well chilled, in a white-wine glass.
value.avoid: Avoid oaky Chardonnay and tannic reds: artichoke makes oak taste sweet and tannin metallic, and oak plus cream sauce turns heavy.
value.zeroProofWhy: basil and lime echo the tarragon and cut the cream.

It sits with a Creole-spiced potato and a soft-boiled egg, so the yolk runs into everything. Then two sauces: hollandaise for richness, and marchand de vin, a savory red wine and mushroom sauce that doubles down on the braise. Think of it as steak and eggs, New Orleans style.

Pepper and dried herbs pick up the Creole spice, and the fruit rounds the heat. The finish is savory, juicy and warm.

value.s45: This is chicken and waffles gone luxurious. The duck leg is confit, cured and cooked slowly in its own fat until it’s tender, with crisp skin. It sits on a savory cornbread and chive waffle, and the foie gras butter melts in for extra richness. Mustard maple syrup brings sweet with a little tang to balance all that, and a sunny-side-up egg ties it together. Sweet, savory, rich, it’s a showstopper for a brunch guest who wants something different.

value.why: Riesling’s acidity cuts the duck fat and foie gras butter, and its ripe fruit meets the maple syrup.
value.sayIt: With the duck and maple, the Berres Riesling is lovely, bright acidity for the richness, ripe fruit for the syrup.
value.whyThisWine: It’s rich duck with maple syrup, so I want brightness and a touch of fruit. This German Riesling cuts the richness and loves the maple, it keeps every bite fresh.
value.palate: Confit fat and foie gras butter coat the palate; Riesling’s high acidity cuts straight through and refreshes. Maple syrup would make a dry, tannic red taste thin and bitter, but the Riesling’s ripe stone fruit keeps pace with the sweetness, and the mustard’s tang is echoed by the wine’s acidity. The result is sweet-savory balance: rich duck, bright wine, and syrup that tastes fruity rather than cloying.
value.secondWhy: Pinot Noir and duck is a classic, for a guest who wants red.
value.serve: The Berres is off-dry, so lead with it; taste the open bottle at lineup if the vintage has changed. Well chilled, white-wine glass, poured as the dish fires.

Louisiana shrimp go on top in Creole sauce, a tomato-based sauce with the holy trinity of onion, celery and bell pepper, with tasso, a smoky, spiced Cajun ham, for depth. Fried okra chips add crunch. value.sayIt: With the shrimp and grits, the Minuty rosé is perfect, dry and refreshing, great with the tomato and a little spice.

It’s topped with Louisiana lump crab, the sweet, meaty pieces from the body of the crab. The sauce is a pecan bordelaise, so it’s nutty and savory. Underneath, a silky cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens, which bring a little earthiness. Lighter than the egg dishes but still very satisfying.

value.why: A creamy, cool-climate Chardonnay meets the pecans, crab and purée, and keeps enough acidity for the fish and greens.
value.sayIt: I’d pour the Gainey Chardonnay, creamy enough for the pecans and crab, fresh enough for the fish.

Its acidity keeps the delicate fish in focus and brightens the sweet crab. Against the collards’ mild bitterness, the wine’s ripe fruit rounds the edges, and the finish lands on citrus rather than butter, rich but lifted.

A sunny-side-up egg from Vital Farms gives you a runny yolk, and béarnaise, butter, egg yolk, shallot and tarragon, is the classic steak sauce. How would you like it cooked?

The smoked pavé picks up the wine’s savory side, finishing beefy and clean.

The sauce is Foyot, fwah-YO, which is béarnaise, the tarragon butter sauce, made even richer with a reduced meat glaze. Roasted and glazed summer squash balances it. It’s a celebration dish, and with a side of mushrooms or the shells and cheese, it’s a full feast for two.

value.sayIt: For the Chateaubriand, we pour the 2010 Inglenook Rubicon by the glass, a Napa legend with real age on it, powerful but silky. Or I can bring our sommelier for a red Burgundy from our cellar.
value.whyThisWine: The Rubicon is a Napa legend with sixteen years of age. It’s powerful, but the age has made it silky, so it flatters the tenderness of the beef and loves the rich Foyot sauce.
value.palate: Tenderloin is lean, so a young, firm Cabernet would dry the palate. Here age has softened the tannin; it binds with the Foyot’s butter and the beef’s protein and feels round. The meat glaze’s savory depth meets the wine’s tertiary earth and tobacco, while its cassis fruit gives the mild beef a lift. Acidity cuts the béarnaise, and the finish stays long, savory and silky.
value.secondWhy: For finesse over power: a Premier Cru red Burgundy, tenderloin is delicate, and Pinot Noir lets it shine.

The grapes are pickled with hibiscus, so they’re sweet, tart and floral. dishes.name: World Famous Bananas Foster
dishes.serviceNote: Minimum 2 people per order ($14). Seed it with the entrée order. The printed menu says rum; Brennan’s own published recipe also uses banana liqueur, follow the house procedure you’re trained on. TABLESIDE SAFETY: (1) Set the cart where nothing hangs overhead and away from drapes, décor and air vents; clear menus, napkins and paper from it. (2) Guests seated and back from the cart; no one leaning in; watch children, loose sleeves and long hair. (3) Measure the rum into a small vessel first, never pour from the bottle near a flame. (4) Pull the pan off the flame to add rum, then tilt the far edge toward the flame to ignite, away from you and the guests. (5) Never add alcohol to a lit pan. (6) Keep a lid or cover within reach to smother, and know where the extinguisher is. (7) Let the flame burn out before plating; turn the burner off before you leave the cart. Flambéing doesn’t remove all the alcohol, tell guests who avoid it. Dairy (butter, ice cream); ice cream likely contains egg. On the breakfast tasting it comes with Congregation Coffee & Chicory.

kept.q: Does the recipe use banana liqueur as well as rum?

kept.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?
kept.a: Rum, butter, brown sugar and flambeed caramel sit in the caramel and nut group, whose textbook partners are oxidative fortifieds, so Banyuls Reserva would lead and the Auslese would be the bright second for contrast. The Auslese stays first in this pack because the Banyuls is a tasting pour and is not confirmed a la carte; nothing changes until that answer exists.

value.s10: The Spoonbill: Hendrick's gin and Cap Corse Mattei Blanc quinquina with chive oil, served with a spoon of caviar.
value.s20: The Spoonbill is the grandest of our three luxury cocktails: Hendrick's gin with Cap Corse Mattei Blanc, a Corsican quinquina aperitif, and chive oil, served with a spoon of caviar. Savory, cool and elegant, only in the Roost Bar.
value.s45: The Spoonbill is the grandest of the three luxury cocktails in our Roost Bar. It's Hendrick's, a Scottish gin with cucumber and rose, with Cap Corse Mattei Blanc, a Corsican quinquina, which is an aperitif wine with a gentle bitterness, and chive oil for a savory, green note. It comes with a spoon of caviar, so you taste cool gin and then the salt of the caviar. It's $36.00, a martini drinker's treat.

cocktails.name: Thompson’s Dream
cocktails.note: Printed in the guide only inside the Classic Sazerac service note (pdf p39) with its build and price; the cocktails page shows the Sazerac's premium variations at $20.00 and $40.00. No measures, glass or garnish printed: the build follows the Classic, so confirm with the bar.

say.value: Willett is WILL-it; St. George is saint JORJ.

guest.value: Our Sazerac stepped up: Willett 4-year rye, Bitter Truth Creole Bitters and a St. George absinthe rinse.

why.value: The Sazerac ladder's middle rung at $20: offer it whenever a guest orders a second Sazerac.

origin.value: The name is the house's own; no Willett bottling carries it, so say it is probably named for Thompson Willett, who founded the Willett distillery in Bardstown in 1936.

value.technique: built in the Sazerac pattern into a glass rinsed with St. George absinthe; the measures are not printed
value.sauce: Bitter Truth Creole Bitters, St. George absinthe rinse
value.taste: louder rye spice and more heat than the Classic, with a greener, more herbal rinse

value.s10: Thompson's Dream: our Sazerac stepped up, with Willett rye, Bitter Truth Creole Bitters and a St. George absinthe rinse.
value.s20: Thompson's Dream is the first step up from our Classic Sazerac: Willett 4-year rye with Bitter Truth Creole Bitters, in a glass rinsed with St. George absinthe. Spicier and bolder, for a guest who already loves Sazeracs.
value.s45: If you love the Sazerac, Thompson's Dream is the next rung. We use Willett 4-year rye, from a family distillery in Bardstown, Kentucky, which runs spicier and stronger than the classic's rye. The bitters are Bitter Truth Creole Bitters, made in Munich in the Creole style, and the glass is rinsed with St. George absinthe, the first American absinthe made legally after the old ban. Louder spice, a greener rinse, and it's $20. For a nightcap, our Roost Bar pours the Birdcage, a smoked Old Fashioned.

cocktails.name: Origin Story
cocktails.note: Printed in the guide only inside the Classic Sazerac service note (pdf p39) with its build and price, the highest cocktail price the guide prints. No measures, glass or garnish printed; which Dudognon, and who ages the bitters, are lineup questions.

say.value: Dudognon is doo-doh-NYOHN; Jade Nouvelle-Orléans is ZHAHD noo-VEL or-lay-AHN.

guest.value: The Sazerac the way it began, on Cognac: Dudognon, barrel-aged Peychaud's and Jade Nouvelle-Orléans absinthe.

why.value: The top of the Sazerac ladder at $40: offer it at the Chateaubriand table or after the dinner tasting.

origin.value: The first Sazeracs were Cognac and Peychaud's; rye took over once phylloxera made Cognac scarce in the 1870s and 1880s, so say the way it began, Cognac and Peychaud's, rather than the way it was first made.

value.technique: built in the Sazerac pattern on Cognac with Jade absinthe; the measures are not printed
value.taste: rounder than the Classic: grape, dried fruit and oak, a softer bitters note and a floral wormwood aroma

value.s10: Origin Story: the Sazerac on Cognac, the way it began, with Dudognon, barrel-aged Peychaud's and Jade absinthe.
value.s20: Origin Story is our top Sazerac: Dudognon Cognac with barrel-aged Peychaud's and Jade Nouvelle-Orléans absinthe. The first Sazeracs were Cognac and Peychaud's, so this is the drink the way it began, rounder and richer.
value.s45: Origin Story is the Sazerac the way it began. The first Sazeracs were Cognac and Peychaud's, before rye took over, so we use Dudognon, a family estate in Grande Champagne, Cognac's first growth, with Peychaud's bitters rested in a barrel and Jade Nouvelle-Orléans absinthe, created by a New Orleans native as a tribute to the city's old absinthe houses. It's rounder than the classic: grape, dried fruit and oak with a floral finish. It's $40. After dinner, come up to the Roost Bar for the Birdcage, our smoked Old Fashioned.

value.s45: Our Bloody Mary is one of the classic eye openers, the morning drinks New Orleans is known for. It comes with pickled okra and spicy beans, so you get a pickled crunch with the savory, tangy drink. It's the one to choose if you don't eat beef, because our other classic, the Bloody Bull, is the same idea with beef bouillon stirred in for a richer, meatier drink. Ask me about the spice level and I'll check with the bar.

value.s45: At Bubbles at Brennan's, our afternoon Champagne service in the Roost Bar and courtyard, the house cocktail is Brennan's Champagne Cocktail at $20. The classic version, printed back in 1862, is a sugar cube soaked in bitters with dry Champagne poured over it, so it keeps fizzing from the bottom up, and some bars add a splash of Cognac. Our bar has its own build, and I'll tell you exactly what's in it. If you're here on a Friday at 5, stay for the sabering.

cocktails.name: New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory
cocktails.note: Priced in the guide's Eye openers and coffee must-know (pdf p49): one $11 is printed before all three coffees, so whether each is $11 is a lineup question. The breakfast tasting pours it as Brennan's Private Blend Congregation Coffee and Chicory.

guest.value: Our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory: dark, roasty and smooth, with a gentle bitterness.

why.value: The guide's zero-proof pick for the sweet plates: the French toast, the coffee cake, Bananas Foster, Cherries Jubilee, the bread pudding and the Snickers.

origin.value: Chicory is the roasted root of Cichorium intybus; the New Orleans habit is usually traced to Civil War blockade shortages, with a French precedent. It adds body and a cocoa-like bitterness and no caffeine.

value.main: coffee blended with roasted chicory root
value.technique: brewed hot, New Orleans style
value.sauce: chicory: roasty, gently bitter, almost chocolatey
value.sides: served hot; ask how the guest takes it
value.taste: dark, roasty and smooth, with a gentle bitterness that balances dessert

value.s10: Our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory: roasty, smooth and gently bitter, the classic with dessert.
value.s20: Our coffee is New Orleans style, blended with chicory, a roasted root the city has added to its coffee for generations. It's dark, roasty and smooth, and its gentle bitterness is perfect with Bananas Foster or bread pudding.
value.s45: New Orleans coffee means coffee with chicory. Chicory is a roasted root; the city's habit is usually traced to wartime shortages in the 1860s, and it stuck because it adds body and a cocoa-like bitterness without any caffeine of its own. Our breakfast tasting pours Brennan's private blend from Congregation Coffee, an Algiers Point roaster. It's dark and smooth, and that bitterness is exactly what balances sweet desserts like the Bananas Foster, the bread pudding or the Snickers.

value.s45: For a guest who wants coffee on its own terms, we pour a single-origin coffee from Congregation Coffee, a roaster in Algiers Point, across the river from the French Quarter. Single origin means the beans come from one place, so the cup tastes of that place rather than a blend, and there's no chicory, so it's cleaner and brighter than our New Orleans-style coffee. Congregation rotates its origins with the seasons, so I'll read you today's from the coffee card.

value.s20: Café Glacé de la Maison is our house iced coffee: chicory cold brew sweetened with a cardamom and clove syrup, under an orange flower foam. Cold, roasty, gently spiced and floral, and no alcohol.
value.s45: Café glacé is French for iced coffee, and ours is the house version. We start with chicory cold brew, so it's smooth and roasty, sweeten it with a syrup of cardamom and clove, the clove a nod to the city's flamed café brûlot, and top it with an orange flower foam. It's cold, lightly sweet and fragrant. It's lovely with the baked apple or the duck confit waffle, and it's the drink for anyone skipping the milk punch.

toGuest.value: Eggs Hussarde is New Orleans’ answer to Eggs Benedict, with a red wine sauce as well as hollandaise.
Eggs Sardou is the New Orleans egg dish with artichokes and creamed spinach.
Marchand de vin is a savory red wine and mushroom sauce; it gives the eggs a deep, rich note.
Hollandaise is the buttery, lemony egg-yolk sauce you know from Eggs Benedict.
Béarnaise is a rich butter sauce with tarragon, the classic sauce for steak.
Choron is a béarnaise with tomato, tangy and herbal.
Sauce Foyot is béarnaise made even richer with a reduced beef glaze.
Débris is meltingly tender, slow-cooked meat in its own gravy.
Véronique means fish with grapes, ours are pickled with hibiscus.
En papillote means in paper; here we use a banana leaf instead, so the fish steams in its own juices and stays moist.
Beurre blanc is a silky white wine and butter sauce.
Poussin à la moutarde means young chicken with mustard.
’Nduja is a spicy, spreadable Italian sausage that melts into the beans.
Persillade is a fresh parsley-and-garlic topping, ours has pumpkin seeds for crunch.
Mignonette is the classic raw bar sauce for oysters, vinegar, shallot and cracked pepper; ours has preserved Fresno chili.
The egg yolk is cured and grated over the top, like bottarga, it adds a rich, salty finish.
Brabant potatoes are New Orleans’ crispy cubed potatoes.
Milk punch is our classic breakfast cocktail: brandy, cream, vanilla and nutmeg.
A Bloody Bull is a Bloody Mary with beef broth, savory and rich.
Chicory is a roasted root we blend into our coffee, the New Orleans way.
Café brûlot is New Orleans’ spiced, flamed coffee, the cake borrows its flavors.

say.value: TAH-so (TASS-oh is also heard; confirm the house habit)

toGuest.value: Tasso is Cajun spiced, cured and smoked pork, used to season the sauce.
Popcorn rice is a Louisiana rice with a nutty, toasty aroma.
Tarte Tatin is the French upside-down caramelized tart, ours is pineapple.

say.value: ERB-sant (ERB-saint also heard); never sound the H

toGuest.value: Herbsaint is the anise liqueur created in New Orleans in 1934, just a rinse in the Sazerac glass for aroma.
Framboise is French for raspberry; the French toast is finished with raspberry coulis and local raspberries.
Fines herbes is the classic French mix of delicate herbs, parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, on the crab claws.
Mimolette is a bright orange French cheese from Lille, nutty and a little sweet as it ages, dyed with annatto; it makes the fondue on the shells and cheese.
Pralines are the New Orleans pecan and brown sugar candies crumbled over the bread pudding.
Rösti is the Swiss grated potato cake under the petite filet on the breakfast tasting.
Mascarpone is a rich Italian cream cheese, whipped into a light mousse for the French toast.
Shiitake are the savory Japanese mushrooms, preserved, on the blackened tofu.
Burrata is fresh mozzarella with a creamy center, on the Creole tomato tostada.
Grana Padano is a hard, nutty Italian cheese like Parmesan, on the Caesar and the shells and cheese.
Castelvetrano olives are the bright green, mild and buttery Sicilian olives in the papillote.
Gremolata is a fresh chopped topping; ours is Marcona almond with lemon and basil on the crab and corn omelette.
Harissa is the North African chili paste that seasons the smoked cauliflower.
Yuzu is a fragrant Japanese citrus; its mousse is the heart of the lemon tart.
Chateaubriand is the thick center cut of the beef tenderloin, roasted for two.
Confit is meat cured and cooked slowly in its own fat until tender; the duck leg on the waffle.
Pavé means paving stone; the smoked potato pavé is layered potato pressed and cut into a neat block.
Andouille is the smoky Louisiana pork sausage in the gumbo.
Gumbo is the Louisiana stew built on a dark roux; ours is seafood with andouille over popcorn rice.
Luxardo is the Italian family house famous for maraschino cherries and the liqueur, founded in 1821 and in Italy since 1947; its sauce dresses the Cherries Jubilee.

Peychaud's is the bright red New Orleans bitters with anise and cherry notes in the Sazerac; the story puts Antoine Peychaud's pharmacy a few doors up Royal Street, so confirm it at lineup before telling it.
The Sazerac is New Orleans' official cocktail: ours is rye stirred with Peychaud's in a glass rinsed with Herbsaint, and the first Sazeracs were made on Cognac, as our Origin Story is.
Crème fraîche is a slightly tangy cultured cream, sweetened on the baked apple and whipped on the coffee cake.
Financiers are small, buttery almond cakes; the blackberry ones give the trifle its texture.
A bavarois, or Bavarian, is a set cream; the Snickers starts with a Bavarian milk chocolate.
Paul Blangé was the house's first chef, who led the kitchen until the 1970s and created Bananas Foster and Eggs Hussarde.
Escoffier was the great French chef who wrote down sauce Foyot and made Cherries Jubilee for Queen Victoria.
The guéridon is the cart the Bananas Foster is made on at your table.
Fresno is a red Californian chili from the 1950s, about the heat of a jalapeño but fruitier; preserved in the mignonette it gives a gentle warmth, not real heat.
Creole is New Orleans city cooking, French and Spanish at the root with more butter, cream and sauces; Cajun is the country cooking of Acadiana, one pot, dark roux and spicier. Brennan's is Creole.

Pierre Sparr is an Alsace house; its sparkling rosé is all Pinot Noir, made like Champagne, dry with bright berry fruit.
Charles Lafitte is the crisp, dry Champagne poured on both tasting menus, a house with roots to 1834 in the Vranken-Pommery group.
C.H. Berres is an old Mosel family estate at Ürzig; its Old Vines Riesling is our off-dry glass for spice and for the duck waffle.
Pazo das Bruxas, the manor of the witches, is Familia Torres's Albariño from Spain's Atlantic coast, citrusy with a salty edge.

Domaine Durand is our Loire Sauvignon Blanc, crisp and herbal, the wine that loves artichokes.

toGuest.value: Gainey is a Santa Barbara County estate; its Chardonnay is creamy but fresh, our first pick for the butter sauces.
Domaine Leflaive is one of Burgundy's great white wine estates, famous for Puligny-Montrachet; we pour its Mâcon by the glass by Coravin.
Mâcon-Verzé is the village appellation in southern Burgundy where Leflaive makes this Chardonnay.
Domaine Fichet is a family estate at Igé in the Mâconnais; its Château London is a named vineyard parcel, no castle and nothing to do with England.
Mâcon-Igé is the village appellation of the Fichet Chardonnay poured with the lobster on the dinner tasting.

Damien Martin runs his family's domaine at Davayé in the Mâconnais; his Bourgogne Pinot Noir is our light, silky red by the glass.

Beaune is the wine capital of Burgundy and the village behind the Jadot Premier Cru on the tasting.
Beaumes-de-Venise is a Southern Rhône village famous for sweet Muscat; the Durban we pour is its dry red, ripe Grenache with Syrah.
Domaine de Durban is the Beaumes-de-Venise estate behind our ripe, soft Southern Rhône red.
Domaine de Châteaumar makes the Cuvée Vincent Côtes du Rhône poured with the filet at breakfast: old vine Syrah from beside Châteauneuf-du-Pape, juicy and soft.
Moulin d'Issan is the Bordeaux from the Château d'Issan team in Margaux, Merlot led with Cabernet, cassis and cedar for the steak.
Rubicon is Inglenook's flagship Napa Cabernet from Rutherford; our 2010 has sixteen years of age, powerful but silky, $70 the glass.
Paul Hobbs is the Napa winemaker whose Coombsville Cabernet is poured with the duck on the dinner tasting.
Coombsville is one of Napa's cooler corners, near the town of Napa, so its Cabernet keeps its freshness.
Dr. Hermann is the Mosel estate behind our sweet Erdener Prälat Auslese, the $80 half-bottle for dessert.
Erdener Prälat is one of the Mosel's famous steep vineyards, the source of our Auslese.
Auslese means selected harvest, a tier above late harvest Spätlese: sweet, honeyed Riesling with bright acidity.
La Tour Vieille is the Banyuls estate whose Reserva, fig, caramel and coffee, is the dessert pour on the dinner tasting.
Banyuls is a sweet fortified red from the schist terraces of Roussillon, at least half Grenache, the classic with chocolate.
Coravin lets us pour a single glass and keep the bottle fresh: a needle through the cork for the Leflaive, a sparkling stopper on the opened bottle for the Rare.

Creekstone Farms is Black Angus beef from a Kansas producer; the breakfast hanger is USDA Prime.
Vital Farms is pasture raised eggs; every hen gets over a hundred square feet of grass.
Rohan is a special cross bred for the D'Artagnan company and raised in New York's Hudson Valley for tender, rosy meat.

Our mushroom side; the kitchen says which mushrooms and how they are cooked tonight.

Monkey 47 is a Black Forest gin bottled at 47 percent, with a big botanical lift; it goes into the Flamingo.
Chopin is a Polish potato vodka, smooth and round; it goes into the Flamingo.
Taittinger is one of the great Champagne houses; its La Française is the Champagne in the Flamingo.
Rabbit Hole Dareringer is a Kentucky straight bourbon from Louisville, finished in PX sherry casks; it is the base of the Birdcage.
Cap Corse Mattei Blanc is a Corsican quinquina, a wine aperitif with a gentle bitterness; it goes into the Spoonbill.
