scenarios.title: Foster for one
scenarios.guest: Just me, can I get the Bananas Foster?

you.value: It’s made in one pan at the table for at least two people, so the minimum order is two. If you’d like a flambé just for you, Cherries Jubilee is also finished at the table, let me check with the kitchen on a single order. And the Dulce de Leche is the Foster in a glass.

principle.value: Explain the reason for the rule, then offer an alternative with the same theater, and check before you promise. Confirm at lineup whether a single Cherries Jubilee is possible before offering it, so you are not promising twice.

scenarios.title: No alcohol
scenarios.guest: We don’t drink. Can we still have the Bananas Foster? Doesn’t the alcohol burn off?

you.value: Some of it burns off, but most of it stays, so I wouldn’t recommend it if you avoid alcohol completely. The Lemon Tart or the Pineapple Tarte Tatin are wonderful, and for a drink, our spirit-free Catalina Island is watermelon and tonic.

principle.value: Be accurate about alcohol; never promise it ‘all cooks off.’ Also watch the turtle soup (Sherry), bread pudding (whiskey caramel) and shells & cheese (beer).

scenarios.title: Vegetarian at dinner
scenarios.guest: I’m vegetarian. What can I have?

you.value: The Creole Tomato Tostada to start, then the Blackened Tofu, it’s local Tien Dat tofu with rice grits and shiitakes, and the Smoked Cauliflower on the side. Let me confirm with the kitchen about butter and stocks. At breakfast: Eggs Sardou or the Framboise French Toast, with the same check.

principle.value: Name a full meal, then verify the hidden animal products (butter, stock, gelatin, bouillon in the Bloody Bull, bacon in the succotash).

scenarios.title: Shellfish allergy
scenarios.guest: I’m allergic to shellfish.

you.value: Thank you for telling me. I’m writing it on the ticket and the chef will go through your choices with me. Where the menu lists shellfish: on both menus, the gumbo and the Creole Caesar’s smoked oyster dressing; at breakfast and lunch, the Louisiana Oysters, the Pecan Gulf Fish with crab, the Crab & Corn Omelette and the Shrimp & Grits; at dinner, the Grand Isle Jewel Oysters, the Louisiana Crab Claws, the Gulf Fish en Papillote with crab, and the Louisiana BBQ Lobster on the tasting. Give me two minutes and I’ll come back with what the chef is happy to send.

principle.value: Name what the menu prints, never what is probably fine; the kitchen clears the dish, not you; flag the ticket and tell the captain.

scenarios.title: Chateaubriand wine
scenarios.guest: We’re sharing the Chateaubriand. What should we drink?

you.value: Two directions: by the glass, the 2010 Inglenook Rubicon: Napa Cabernet with sixteen years of age, so it’s powerful but silky, $70. Or, for elegance, a red Burgundy from our cellar, I’d love to bring our sommelier over to pick one with you.

principle.value: Give two styles and a clear price, and use the cellar and sommelier as a resource.

scenarios.title: Celebration
scenarios.guest: It’s our anniversary, something special to start?

you.value: Congratulations! We pour a prestige vintage Champagne by the glass: Rare, kept fresh under a Coravin stopper, at $75. For something lighter, our house Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut. And if you’re here on a Friday at 5, we saber Champagne in the courtyard.

principle.value: Match the moment with a special pour and a Brennan’s ritual. Check the vintage and the sabering schedule before you say either.

scenarios.title: Shellfish and nuts at one table
scenarios.guest: My husband is allergic to shellfish and I’m allergic to tree nuts.

you.value: Thank you both. It goes on the ticket and the chef walks through your choices with me before I promise anything. The menu lists shellfish in the gumbo, the Caesar dressing, the oysters, the crab dishes and the shrimp; and nuts in the pecan fish, the omelette, the papillote, the duck and the coffee cake. Two minutes with the kitchen.

principle.value: Name what is printed, let the kitchen give the final answer, flag the ticket, tell the captain.

scenarios.title: Pregnant guest and raw oysters
scenarios.guest: I’m pregnant. Are the oysters OK?

you.value: The Grand Isle oysters are served raw, and the menu carries the advisory that raw shellfish carries a risk, especially in pregnancy. I can’t advise you medically, so that’s your call. For the same brininess cooked, the Crab Claws come warm in brown butter, and at breakfast the Louisiana Oysters are cooked in BBQ sauce.

principle.value: State the advisory, never decide for the guest, never moralize, have a cooked alternative ready.

scenarios.title: Vegan at breakfast
scenarios.guest: I’m vegan. What can I have?

you.value: Honestly, our breakfast is built on eggs and butter, so I won’t guess. The chef can usually build something and I’d rather ask her than improvise. Grits, Brabant potatoes and the fruit starters are where she usually starts, and every one needs a question about butter or dairy.

principle.value: Honesty, then the kitchen, never a guessed plate.

scenarios.title: Gluten
scenarios.guest: I avoid gluten.

you.value: The obvious ones are the English muffins, the biscuit, the French toast and the bread pudding. Where it hides I won’t guess: the soups may be roux based, the artichokes and the grit cake are fried, and the fryer and the blackening spice need a question. Let me have the kitchen go through it with me.

principle.value: Separate the obvious from the hidden; send the hidden to the kitchen.

scenarios.title: A child at the table
scenarios.guest: Anything for a six-year-old?

you.value: Yes, our children's menu is for ten and under, $25.00 for three courses with a drink. If she likes things plain, the grilled cheese or the buttered noodles; at breakfast, the vanilla French toast with berries and whipped cream. I'll put her order in first so it comes out quickly, and when the Bananas Foster is lit she'll love it from her seat; we keep little ones back from the cart.

principle.value: Child's order in first and out fast; cart distance; make the flame a treat. Read from the children's card for the meal and confirm today's kid's drink.

scenarios.title: Creole versus Cajun
scenarios.guest: What’s the difference between Creole and Cajun?

you.value: Creole is New Orleans city cooking: French and Spanish at the root, African and Caribbean hands in it, more butter, cream and tomato, more sauces. Cajun is the country cooking of Acadiana, from the Acadian exiles, one pot, dark roux, rustic and spicier. Brennan’s is Creole. You’ll hear me say Cajun for a few ingredients, like the tasso in the shrimp and grits.

principle.value: Two sentences, then back to the menu.

scenarios.title: The tourist who wants the one thing
scenarios.guest: We’re here once. What do we order?

you.value: At breakfast, the Traditional Breakfast at $80 is the whole story: milk punch, baked apple, turtle soup or gumbo with a Bloody Bull, Eggs Hussarde, a petite filet, and Bananas Foster at the table, drinks included. À la carte, it’s the Turtle Soup, the Eggs Hussarde and the Bananas Foster for two.

principle.value: One clear answer, then a shorter one.

scenarios.title: Bananas Foster alone, at dinner
scenarios.guest: I’m dining alone and I came for the Bananas Foster.

you.value: You came to the right place. It’s made in one pan for two, so the order is for two; that’s the pan, not a rule about company. If you’d like the full flame for one, I’ll ask whether we can do a single Cherries Jubilee tonight, and the Dulce de Leche is the Foster in a glass.

principle.value: The reason, the same theater, check before promising, a small consolation.

scenarios.title: A cheaper bottle for the Chateaubriand
scenarios.guest: Seventy dollars a glass is more than we want to spend.

you.value: Absolutely. The Moulin d’Issan Bordeaux at $16 has the cassis and cedar for the beef, and the Durban Southern Rhône at $18 is riper and softer. For a bottle, let me bring our sommelier with the list; tell her roughly where you’d like to land and she’ll find the best value there.

principle.value: Two prices from the list, then the list and the sommelier; never a bottle price from memory; the guest names the budget privately.

scenarios.title: In a hurry before a tour
scenarios.guest: We have a swamp tour at one. Can we be out in forty-five minutes?

you.value: Yes, if we order now and I put the whole table in at once. I’d steer you to the egg dishes and the soup rather than the Chateaubriand or the flambé today, and I’ll bring the check with your last course.

principle.value: Ask the clock, set the pace, tell the kitchen, bring the check early.

scenarios.title: A birthday
scenarios.guest: It’s my mother’s birthday.

you.value: Happy birthday to her. A little fuss, or something quieter? I can pour her a glass of the Rare Champagne to start, and the Bananas Foster is made at the table for the two of you, which is the best candle we have.

principle.value: Loud or quiet first; note it on the ticket.

scenarios.title: Turtle soup too rich
scenarios.guest: This is too rich for me.

you.value: I’m sorry, that’s on me for not saying how rich it is. Let me take it away. The gumbo is lighter and brinier, or the Creole Caesar if you’d like something crisp. Either is on me to swap.

principle.value: The five A’s: awareness, acknowledgement, apology, action, additional generosity (Danny Meyer, Setting the Table, 2006). Tell the manager so the comp is recorded.

scenarios.title: A wine sent back
scenarios.guest: This doesn’t taste right.

you.value: Thank you for saying so. I’ll take it away and bring a fresh glass, or something different if you’d prefer. Shall I bring our sommelier to taste it with you?

principle.value: Never debate a send back; tell the sommelier so a faulty by the glass bottle is pulled before it reaches another table.

scenarios.title: A Sazerac on the rocks
scenarios.guest: Sazerac on the rocks, please.

you.value: Of course. The classic here is served without ice in a chilled glass rinsed with Herbsaint, so it stays spirit forward; over ice it softens as it sits. Let me ask the bar to build it on a large cube for you.

principle.value: Say the classic once, then make the guest’s drink the guest’s way. The over ice build is expert knowledge, not the guide’s; the guide tells you to confirm the bar’s build, so ask.

scenarios.title: Ketchup with the Brabant potatoes
scenarios.guest: Could I get some ketchup for the potatoes?

you.value: Of course, right away.

principle.value: A ramekin, without a flicker.

scenarios.title: Is the tofu vegan?
scenarios.guest: Is the Blackened Tofu vegan?

you.value: Good question, and I’d rather check than guess. Blackening is traditionally done with butter, and I want to confirm the rice grits are cooked without stock. One moment with the kitchen.

principle.value: The guide flags exactly these two questions; defer every time.

scenarios.title: What is Blender’s Reserve?
scenarios.guest: What’s Brennan’s Blender’s Reserve rum?

you.value: Don Q is a Puerto Rican rum house, and the menu lists that rum as a Brennan’s reserve blend. I don’t want to tell you the story wrong, so let me ask our bar manager how it was chosen.

principle.value: Say what the menu prints, nothing more, until lineup confirms.

scenarios.title: Is Eggs Owen for Owen Brennan?
scenarios.guest: Is Eggs Owen named after Owen Brennan?

you.value: Owen Brennan founded the restaurant in 1946, so it’s a fair guess, but the menu doesn’t say and I’d rather not invent it. What I can tell you is the plate: short rib braised in red wine, a Creole spiced potato and a soft boiled egg with both sauces.

principle.value: Never an unconfirmed house story; pivot to the plate.

scenarios.title: Dress code for tonight
scenarios.guest: My son only has shorts with him.

you.value: Our dinner code is dressy casual, jackets preferred, and we ask guests to avoid athletic or cut-off shorts, sleeveless or decal T-shirts, hats and open-toed shoes for men. Let me ask the manager what’s workable tonight so there’s no surprise at the door.

principle.value: Say the code, hand enforcement to the host stand.

scenarios.title: One tasting, one à la carte
scenarios.guest: I’ll do the tasting menu and she’ll order à la carte. Does that work?

you.value: Let me check with the kitchen on tonight’s pacing; a tasting runs five courses and I want your plates to land with them. The Chateaubriand isn’t ideal for a split table because it’s for two.

principle.value: Pacing is a kitchen question; protect both guests from waiting.

scenarios.title: Is the gumbo hot?
scenarios.guest: Is the gumbo spicy?

you.value: Mild to moderate: smoky andouille and a gentle warmth, not heat. I can bring hot sauce, or if you’re spice shy the turtle soup has none.

principle.value: The guide’s spice words, and both directions.

scenarios.title: The sabering
scenarios.guest: You cut Champagne open with a sword?

you.value: We do, in the courtyard, during Bubbles at Brennan’s; the guide says Fridays at 5. It’s a bar team ritual, so be in the courtyard a few minutes early. Rosé bottles run from $50 to $125 and there are bar snacks out there.

principle.value: Time, place and price range; never promise who sabers or that it happens every week without confirming.

scenarios.title: Like a Sazerac, but lighter
scenarios.guest: I love a Sazerac, but I'd like something lighter tonight.

you.value: Then I'd go one of two ways. The Yellowstone on our current list is whiskey with lemon, honey and turmeric and Peychaud's Aperitivo, so it shares the Peychaud's name but drinks bright and easy, $18.00. Or the Niagara Falls, gin with Lillet Blanc, tomato water and lemon, crisp and savory, $15.00. And if the Sazerac itself is calling, it's $13.

principle.value: Name what they love about the drink, then offer the same family in a lighter shape with the price of each; say 'current list', because the cocktail list changes with the season.

scenarios.title: What are the luxury cocktails worth?
scenarios.guest: The Roost Bar cocktails cost a lot more. What makes them worth it?

you.value: The bottles and the moment. The Flamingo is Chopin vodka and Monkey 47 gin with dragonfruit, lemon and Taittinger Champagne, $28.00. The Birdcage is a smoked Old Fashioned on Rabbit Hole Dareringer, a bourbon finished in sherry casks, $31.00. The Spoonbill is Hendrick's gin and Cap Corse Mattei Blanc with chive oil, served with a spoon of caviar, $36.00. If you'd rather stay classic, the Sazerac is $13 and Thompson's Dream is $20.

principle.value: Sell the bottles and the theater, never the price: give each drink its one special thing, then name a classic at a lower price so nobody feels pushed.

scenarios.title: A round of brunch cocktails
scenarios.guest: We're celebrating. What should the four of us start with at brunch?

you.value: For a brunch table I'd mix it: a Brandy Milk Punch, our classic eye opener, $12; a Bloody Bull or our Bloody Mary with pickled okra, $13 and $11; and the Miami Beach, sparkling wine with watermelon and citrus, $14.00. If anyone isn't drinking, the Catalina Island is watermelon and tonic, $15. Shall I bring a mix so everyone can taste?

principle.value: Offer a spread across the styles, creamy, savory and sparkling, with one spirit-free choice, and give each price once.

scenarios.title: Not drinking tonight
scenarios.guest: I'm not drinking tonight. What do you have?

you.value: Plenty. The Catalina Island is Seedlip Grove 42, watermelon and tonic, bright and bubbly, $15; the Black Hills is a margarita idea with Lyre's agave, basil and lime, $14, non-alcoholic rather than zero; and our Café Glacé de la Maison is chicory cold brew with cardamom-clove syrup, $11. With dessert, our chicory coffee is the classic. And I'll steer you past the dishes cooked with alcohol, like the Foster and the turtle soup.

principle.value: Treat a spirit-free guest as a guest with a drink order: three real drinks with their prices, honesty that Lyre's is under half a percent, and the dishes cooked with alcohol named before they order.

scenarios.title: What is on the children's menu?
scenarios.guest: What can our seven-year-old have, and how much is it?

you.value: Our children's menu is for ten and under, $25.00 for three courses with a drink. At breakfast it's sliced fresh fruit first, then eggs any style with toast and bacon, popcorn shrimp with Brabant potatoes, vanilla French toast with berries and whipped cream, or a grilled cheese with Brabant potatoes, and a scoop of vanilla ice cream to finish. At dinner it's a salami and cheese starter, then fried Gulf shrimp with French fries, buttered noodles with cheese, sautéed Gulf fish with potato and green beans, or a grilled cheese with French fries, and the same ice cream. I'll check today's kid's drink with the bar.

principle.value: Read the card for the meal they are at: the age, the one price and the three-course shape, then the four plates, and confirm the drink rather than promising one.

difference.value: Eggs Hussarde is the classic: housemade English muffin, coffee-cured Canadian bacon, poached eggs, hollandaise and marchand de vin ($27). Eggs Owen is heartier: red wine-braised short rib débris, Creole-spiced potato and a soft-boiled egg with the same two sauces ($32).

ask.value: Do you want the classic Brennan’s egg dish, or something heartier, more like steak and eggs?

difference.value: Turtle soup is 100% turtle meat with brown butter spinach, grated egg and aged Sherry, rich, dark and savory. The gumbo is seafood, shrimp, crab, oysters, with smoky andouille over popcorn rice. Both $13; the breakfast tasting offers either.

ask.value: Are you in the mood for something rich and classic, or seafood with a little smoke?

difference.value: The breakfast/lunch hanger ($38) is Creekstone Prime with smoked potato pavé, a sunny-side-up egg and béarnaise, steak and eggs. The dinner hanger ($42) has housemade Creole spice, Madeira-glazed broccolini, pepita persillade and chili crisp, spicier, with no egg.

ask.value: Mostly a matter of meal, at dinner, ask: “Do you enjoy a little heat? The chili crisp brings some.”

difference.value: Both are flambéed tableside over housemade vanilla ice cream. Bananas Foster (invented here in 1951) is bananas in butter, brown sugar, cinnamon and rum, rich and caramel. Cherries Jubilee is fresh tart black cherries in Luxardo sauce, brighter and fruitier.

ask.value: Would you like something rich and caramelly, or tart and fruity? Or both, for the table, two flambés.

difference.value: The Louisiana Oysters are the breakfast and lunch starter, $19, cooked in the buttery New Orleans BBQ sauce with pickled collards and a saltine crumble. The Grand Isle Jewel Oysters are the dinner starter, $22, served raw and cold with a preserved Fresno chili mignonette and the raw advisory.

ask.value: Cooked and buttery, or raw and cold?

difference.value: The Pecan Gulf Fish is the breakfast and lunch entrée, $31, with lump crab, pecan bordelaise, cauliflower purée and collards. The Gulf Fish en Papillote is the dinner entrée, $38, steamed in a banana leaf with crab, Castelvetrano olives, tomato, sorghum and Marcona almonds.

ask.value: A rich pecan butter sauce, or the lighter banana leaf parcel with olives and tomato?

difference.value: The Brandy Milk Punch, $12, is the breakfast eye opener: brandy, cream, vanilla bean and nutmeg, cold and creamy. The Dulce de Leche, $14, is the dessert cocktail: Don Q rum, crème de cacao, banana rum butter sauce and cream, the Foster in a glass.

ask.value: To start the morning, or to finish the meal?

body.value: Invented at Brennan’s in 1951: Owen Brennan challenged his sister Ella and chef Paul Blangé to create a banana dessert (the house's own page and Ralph Brennan credit Ella with Blangé; the commission is also called the Metropolitan Crime Commission), named for Richard Foster, Owen’s friend and chairman of the New Orleans Crime Commission. Flambéed tableside, $14, minimum 2 people per order; 2026 is its 75th year.

Two desserts are flambéed at the table: Bananas Foster and Cherries Jubilee. Chef Kris Padalino (executive chef since June 2025) has said she wants to bring back more tableside cooking, ask at training who performs it (server or captain) and learn the house procedure.

Breakfast & lunch (Mon-Fri 9 to 2, Sat-Sun 8 to 2): 7 appetizers (including three sweet starters), 8 entrées, 7 sides. Dinner (nightly 6 to 10): 7 appetizers, 6 entrées, 5 sides at $12. One dessert menu, linked from both. Turtle soup, gumbo and the Creole Caesar appear at both meals.

Tasting portions of each course and all listed drinks included: Brandy Milk Punch eye opener → baked apple → turtle soup or seafood gumbo with a Bloody Bull → Eggs Hussarde with Charles Lafitte Brut (4 oz) → petite filet with Châteaumar Côtes du Rhône (4 oz) → Bananas Foster tableside with Congregation Coffee & Chicory. The page says “Celebrating 80 Years in 2026!”

Grand Isle Jewel oysters → Louisiana BBQ lobster → Redfish Véronique → Rohan duck → The Snickers. Wine pairing supplement $120 (4 oz pours): Charles Lafitte Brut, Fichet Mâcon-Igé 2024, Louis Jadot Beaune 1er Cru 2023, Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet 2021, La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva.

Menus checked 2026-09-26; none carries a date. Dinner is a late-summer menu (Creole tomatoes, summer squash, glazed summer vegetables, peaches) and the cocktail list is themed “Summer Vacations of 1946”, expect a fall change soon.

Brennan's first won the Wine Spectator Grand Award in 1983, lost the cellar to Katrina in 2005 when a month without power cooked about 35,000 bottles, and won it back in 2021 after rebuilding to more than 15,000 bottles, with Burgundy and Champagne the deep end of the list; the Wine Spectator listing shows about 3,600 selections and more than 19,000 bottles, deepest in Burgundy, Bordeaux and California. Confirm the award years from the listing at lineup. The live by-the-glass list (Binwise) pours Rare Brut 2012 and Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin, plus Inglenook Rubicon 2010 at $70. The restaurant’s own “Cocktails & Wine by the Glass” page shows an older, different glass list (e.g., Drouhin Chablis, Peter Michael, Rare 2013), check the list you’re handed on shift.

Classic eye openers: Bloody Bull $13, Brandy Milk Punch $12, Brennan’s Bloody Mary $11 (pickled okra, spicy beans), Brennan’s Irish Coffee $12. Coffee $11: New Orleans-style with chicory, a single-origin Papua New Guinea from Congregation Coffee, and Café Glacé de la Maison (chicory cold brew, cardamom-clove syrup, orange flower foam). Revive cold-pressed juice $10. Congregation roasts in Algiers; read the single origin from the coffee card on shift rather than naming Papua New Guinea from memory.

Roost Bar & Courtyard, Mon-Fri 2 to 6; Champagne sabering Fridays at 5. Rosé bottles $50 to 125 (Mirabelle to Pommery), bubbly cocktails $12 to 20 (Brennan’s Champagne Cocktail $20), and bar snacks: Creole spiced nuts $6, crawfish meat pies with chive rémoulade $16, fries with pink sauce $8, fried pickles $14, popcorn shrimp $15, cheese board $24, Roost Burger $17. The hours are dated 26 September 2026 and disputed (an older guest description gives Tuesday to Friday 2 to 7): confirm on shift. Sabering has been advertised weekly for about a decade; confirm each Friday with the host stand, and check the courtyard is not privately booked before promising it. Mirabelle is Schramsberg's California sparkling rosé, so say sparkling rosé for the bottom of that range and keep the word Champagne for the Pommery.

Catalina Island (Seedlip Grove 42, local watermelon, tonic) $15 and Black Hills (Lyre’s N/A agave, basil purée, lime) $14. Offer them to guests who skip the flambé or the milk punch. Seedlip Grove 42 is 0.0 percent alcohol; Lyre's is labeled under 0.5 percent, so call the Black Hills non-alcoholic, not zero.
Dressy casual; jackets preferred at dinner. No athletic or cut-off shorts, sleeveless or decal T-shirts, hats, or open-toed shoes for men.

Brennan’s opened in 1946 (at 417 Royal Street since 1956) and celebrates 80 years in 2026, with anniversary tasting menus through the year. Owen Brennan died in 1955; the family opened Royal Street in 1956. Brennan's closed in 2013 and reopened in November 2014 under Ralph Brennan and Terry White.

mustKnows.title: Dietary needs: guests note them at the reservation, and the kitchen always confirms

body.value: The kitchen can accommodate most restrictions. Ask guests to note them at the reservation, write them on the ticket, and let the kitchen clear every choice: the kitchen, not the server, says what a dish can do.

Paul Blangé, the chef behind Bananas Foster, led the kitchen until the 1970s. Michael Roussel, who started here in 1956 and trained under Blangé, became executive chef in 1974 and retired in 2005 after 49 years. Lazone Randolph, who began as a dishwasher in 1965, succeeded him in 2005 and gave his name to Chicken Lazone. Slade Rushing ran the kitchen from the 2014 reopening to 2019 and Ryan Hacker from late 2019 to spring 2025. Our executive chef is Kris Padalino, who took over in June 2025 after eight years in this kitchen as pastry chef and executive sous chef; she trained at Le Cordon Bleu in Pasadena and cooked in Los Angeles and Denver before New Orleans.

1795: it was Louisiana's first bank, then the home of Paul Morphy, the chess champion; look for the bank's initials in the balcony ironwork. Owen Brennan opened on Bourbon Street in July 1946 and the house moved here in 1956, after Owen's death in November 1955, with Ella Brennan finding the backing. The family split in November 1973, settled in 1974: Owen's side kept Royal Street, Ella's side took Commander's Palace; Brennan's of Houston belongs to Ella's side, so a guest who ate at Brennan's in Houston ate at a cousin. The house closed on 28 June 2013 and reopened on 25 November 2014 under Ralph Brennan and Terry White after seventeen months of restoration.

Ten turtles were found living in the courtyard during the 2014 renovation and adopted; Slade Rushing named them for sauces: Béchamel, Hollandaise, Espagnole, Tomate and Velouté, then Rémoulade, Ravigote, Bordelaise, Mignonette and Cocktail, the only male. Their return to the fountain in 2015 began the annual Slowest Second Line on Earth. Say it before the guest asks: the turtle soup is not the turtles.

Our by-the-glass list runs to twenty wines: thirteen glass pours from $14 to $75, an $80 half-bottle of Mosel Auslese for dessert, and six wines poured only as part of the tasting menus. If a guest wants one of the tasting wines on its own, ask before promising it. Check the list you are handed on shift: the website shows an older one.

Our wine director is Sam Bortugno, an Advanced Sommelier, in post since September 2023; confirm at lineup that he is on the floor tonight and how to call a sommelier to a table. Braithe Gill is beverage director for the Ralph Brennan Restaurant Group, a certified sommelier and a 2026 James Beard semifinalist; the research also recorded her as Braithe Tidwell, who led the program when the Grand Award was regained in 2021, so do not call her the wine director.

mustKnows.title: The Wine Room and private events

body.value: The Wine Room is our smallest private room, seating 16, in the old carriage house and stables beside the cellar, with a sixteen foot table milled from one sinker cypress; bookings go through the events office on 504-934-3376, with a minimum that depends on the date. Nine bookable spaces, seated and reception: King's 36 and 40, Queen's 24 and 30, Havana 60 and 75, Morphy 12 and 12, Chanteclair 100 and 160, Roost Bar 20 and 30, Audubon 50 and 60, Wine Room 16 and 16, Courtyard 50 and 75; events from 15 to 500. For private parties, corkage is $25 a bottle, a magnum $50 counting as two, six bottles at most; the dining room policy is not published, ask a manager.
Reservations are on OpenTable, open 60 days ahead; parties larger than six ring 504-525-9711.

Royal Street is a pedestrian mall from 11 in the morning, so there is no drop off at the door at lunch; the street is open to cars when breakfast opens and all evening. We validate parking at two garages, 535 Chartres and 716 Iberville, for up to three hours; check the current rates and whether valet is on tonight with the host stand, since the two readings of the FAQ disagree on valet.

Christmas Eve: breakfast and lunch à la carte, dinner 5:30 to 9 with a three course $85 menu. New Year's Eve: breakfast and lunch à la carte, dinner 6 to 10 à la carte. The year is unconfirmed; re-read each season. Réveillon proper is advertised at the sister house Ralph's on the Park; Brennan's frames Christmas Eve as its holiday dinner.
The group runs Brennan's, Napoleon House, Red Fish Grill, Ralph's on the Park, Cafe NOMA, Jazz Kitchen Coastal Grill and Patio, and Beignets Expressed.

mustKnows.title: Who does what on the floor

body.value: Brennan's has captains; staff train for months before cooking Bananas Foster tableside, and a new server does not flame a pan before sign off. Erick Schmitt is general manager per the house's 2026 team directory; confirm the spelling on the page. Who performs the flambé, the Friday sabrage, the Chateaubriand carving, the papillote opening and the Coravin pours, and how the floor is organized, are lineup questions.

For children ten and under, at breakfast and at dinner; the web card read 3 October 2026 prints every item at $25.00, confirm on the live card. On 6 April 2026 we threw a courtyard party for the dessert's 75th birthday: a Champagne sabering, free tastes for the first 75 guests, a flame competition and the crowning of a Banana King.

Breakfast and lunch run 9 to 2 on weekdays and 8 to 2 at weekends, dinner is every night 6 to 10, and Bubbles at Brennan's happy hour is weekdays 2 to 6 in the Roost Bar and Courtyard, with Champagne sabered on Fridays at 5. mustKnows.title: Café Brûlot is a cake, not a drink, on today's menus

body.value: The only Brûlot item is the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake. Café Brûlot Diabolique, the flamed brandy and chicory coffee, was devised at Antoine's by Jules Alciatore around 1890; the house served it in the family era and the cookbook carries a recipe, but it is on no current menu and only two things are flamed at the table, both desserts. history.value: Owen Brennan opened the restaurant on Bourbon Street in July 1946, and it has been at 417 Royal Street since 1956. Owen died in November 1955, before the move; Ella Brennan found the backing and the family opened Royal Street in 1956. The building dates from 1795, was the first bank in Louisiana and later the home of Paul Morphy, the chess champion; the bank's initials survive in the balcony ironwork. The family split in November 1973, settled in 1974: Owen's widow Maude and sons Pip, Jimmy and Ted kept Royal Street, and Ella's side took Commander's Palace. Brennan's closed in June 2013 and reopened in November 2014 under Ralph Brennan and Terry White after a restoration of the whole house. Paul Blange, the first chef, created Bananas Foster and Eggs Hussarde; Michael Roussel, Lazone Randolph, Slade Rushing and Ryan Hacker followed him, and Kris Padalino has led the kitchen since June 2025. 2026 is the 80th year.
